item.title: Direct C(sp3)–H/C(sp2)–F Cross-Coupling of Methylpyridines with Aryl Fluorides
item.description: Direct C(sp3)–H functionalization of methylpyridines is intrinsically challenging. Herein, we report a transition-metal-free, silylboronate-mediated heterobenzylation of methylpyridines with aryl fluorides. The combination of a silylboronate and KOtBu enables direct C(sp3)–H/C(sp2)–F coupling under mild conditions, providing efficient access to structurally diverse azaarylmethanes. The reaction accommodates π-extended aryl fluorides, polyfluoroarenes, and various 4-alkylpyridines, including substrates bearing multiple potentially reactive C–H or C–F bonds, with useful levels of chemo- and regioselectivity. The method is also applicable to the late-stage functionalization of structurally complex molecules. Alkyl fluorides are also compatible via the C(sp3)–H/C(sp3)–F coupling reaction. Mechanistic studies, including aryl-halide comparison, radical-trapping, investigation of pronucleophile, Hammett plot, competition experiments, and DFT calculation support an ionic pathway involving generation of a heterobenzylic nucleophile followed by nucleophilic substitution of the C–F bond. For electronically neutral and electron-rich aryl fluorides, the observed reactivity is consistent with a concerted SNAr pathway. This strategy provides a complementary approach to conventional transition-metal-catalyzed heterobenzylic arylation and expands the synthetic utility of organofluorine compounds as coupling partners for C–C bond formation.

item.title: Comparative Assessment of Degradation Pathways for Enzymatic Degradation of Polybutylene Terephthalate (PBT) and Polyethylene Terephthalate (PET) and their Degradation Intermediates
item.description: Elucidating how polymer chemistry and substrate crystallinity collectively determine polyester degradability is a key to advancing enzymatic recycling as it enables predictive assessment of the degradation behavior of novel substrates and accelerates the development of efficient recycling strategies. Achieving this requires a systematic comparison across different polymer chemistries and crystallinity states. However, direct comparative studies remain scarce. Here, we compare the enzymatic degradation pathways of amorphous and semicrystalline poly(ethylene terephthalate) (PET) and poly(butylene terephthalate) (PBT) using the cutinase LCCiccg. Degradation pathways are characterized through changes in soluble degradation products, surface chemistry and morphology, surface and bulk crystallinity, semicrystalline structures, and mechanical properties. Identified degradation intermediates are synthesized and evaluated for their enzymatic and abiotic hydrolyzability and inhibitory effects on polymer degradation. Across both polymers, enzymatic hydrolysis follows the same cleavage mechanism, whereas substrate crystallinity determines the extent to which degradation can proceed and thereby governs the resulting morphological and mechanical changes. The findings further support a common desorption–readsorption mechanism linking chain accessibility to localized hydrolysis and the persistence of crystalline domains. Collectively, these results reveal two independent axes of transferability: the enzymatic cleavage mechanism is conserved across polymer chemistries, whereas the resulting morphological and mechanical responses are governed primarily by substrate crystallinity.

item.title: How Ready Are Universal Machine-learned Interatomic Potentials for Carbon Capture Simulations?
item.description: Nanoporous materials offer a tunable platform for selective carbon capture through adsorption, and identifying the best candidates requires computational screening built on accurate and transferable models of host–guest interactions. Classical force fields (FFs) have enabled rapid large-scale screening but fail to accurately describe such interactions for challenging systems, and while universal Machine-Learned Interatomic Potentials (u-MLIPs) promise to bridge this gap, their ability to predict macroscopic adsorption observables across chemically diverse frameworks remains largely underexplored. Here we benchmark 25 u-MLIPs against experimental CO2 adsorption data for nine metal–organic frameworks (MOFs) spanning rigid open-pore, open-metal-site, and confined small-pore classes, and find that quantitative isotherm prediction remains out of reach for the evaluated general-purpose models. We show that failures trace to two distinct error sources, the MOF–CO2 and the CO2–CO2 interactions, whose relative contribution shifts with framework chemistry, so that isotherm accuracy cannot be inferred from any single energy metric. In rigid open-pore and confined small-pore MOFs, the MOF–CO2 error dominates, while in strongly interacting frameworks with open metal site (OMS) both MOF–CO2 and CO2–CO2 descriptions become controlling factors, and error cancellation between the two sources can produce simulated accurate isotherms for physically incorrect reasons. Dataset composition, rather than architecture alone, determines whether a model reaches quantitative accuracy, and models trained on explicit MOF–CO2 and multi-molecule CO2 configurations perform most consistently. The evaluation protocol introduced here separates the two error sources and defines concrete paths for advancing u-MLIPs toward reliable computational screening for carbon capture.

item.title: Hessian- and Property-Aware Learning of Analytic Bond-Order Potentials
Gradient ascent pulse engineering (GRAPE)–a primer on quality functions and pulse shape penalties
item.description: Quantum optimal control is a versatile, powerful method to tailor quantum experiments. In NMR, numerical quantum optimal control algorithms such as the gradient ascent pulse engineering (GRAPE) algorithm have sparked many developments in pulse shaping, pushing the limits of pulse selectivity and robustness. To provide an overview of its core principles and the many expansions it has undergone ever since its introduction, the most common quality functions are benchmarked in their ability to guide the spin state transfer for facilitating excitation, inversion, and maximum quantum coherence. Explicit derivations of gradient and Hessian formulas are given, both summarizing what is known from the literature and complementing it. The derivations also give due consideration to the fact that spin states can be represented as density operators or spin operators. Analogously, the most common penalties to guide optimization toward experimentally feasible controls are discussed along with their explicit gradient and Hessian formula derivations. The discussion is complemented by thorough benchmarking for the most commonly used optimization algorithms.

item.title: A Transferable Deprotonated Tyrosine Residue for Amber and CHARMM Force Fields
item.description: The deprotonated form of tyrosine gates proton-coupled electron transfer (PCET) in ribonucleotide reductase and photosystem II, forms the anionic chromophore of fluorescent proteins, and acts as a general acid/base in enzymes, yet a validated, transferable tyrosinate residue for routine fixed-charge protein simulations in the major Amber and CHARMM force fields is lacking. Here, we construct a deprotonated tyrosine residue (TYM) by transferring quinoid phenolate valence parameters, QM-validated for the fluorescent protein chromophore, and phenoxide parameters to standard Amber14/19/99SB* and CHARMM36m force fields. We validate the deprotonated residue against ab initio molecular dynamics simulations of a tyrosine side chain analog in water and experimental protein tyrosine pKa values. The best-performing force fields attain an AUE of roughly 0.5 pK units across 17 residues and preserve the catalytic Tyr57–Tyr16 hydrogen bond in ketosteroid isomerase. Finally, as an application, we combine the parameters with a 2n protonation microstate treatment of residue coupling to obtain a ground-state protonation landscape for the E. coli ribonucleotide reductase radical transfer pathway without introducing radical-specific parameters.

item.title: The Quantification of Ethanol in Exhaled Breath by Proton-Transfer-Reaction Mass Spectrometry
item.description: Proton transfer reaction-time-of-flight-mass spectrometry (PTR-ToF-MS) is used for the real-time, highly sensitive detection and monitoring of volatiles in exhaled breath. However, reliable interpretation of breath volatilome data requires an understanding of the ion-molecule chemistry occurring within the instrument’s drift tube. This is demonstrated in this paper for ethanol, for which quantification based on the observed total product ions to reagent ion signal intensities will be inaccurate owing to the generation of a product ion that is not directly observed, resulting in reduced total product ion signal intensities. In this study, we report the product ion distributions of ethanol as a function of reduced electric field strength under both normal and humid buffer gas operating conditions, with the high humid conditions being more representative for breath analysis. The primary objective is to provide an improved approach for the quantitative determination of ethanol in breath samples. Density functional theory calculations have been used to provide mechanistic insight into the underlying reaction pathways and comparative PTR-ToF-MS measurements are provided of isotopically labelled ethanol isotopologues together with two other alcohols that are commonly present in exhaled breath, namely 1-propanol and 2-propanol. A significant complication in the isotopic studies arises from extensive deuterium-hydrogen exchange between deuterated product ions and H2O, which alters the observed ion distributions under both normal and humid conditions. Collectively, the elements of this study establishes a comprehensive mechanistic framework for ethanol PTR-ToF-MS ion chemistry and demonstrate that accurate quantification of ethanol in exhaled breath requires consideration of primary and secondary product-ion channels that remains experimentally unobserved for ethanol. The findings provide the foundation for the more reliable determination of exhaled ethanol and other primary alcohol concentrations by PTR-ToF-MS that may ultimately reduce, or even eliminate, the need for ethanol-specific instrument calibration which is problematic in clinical settings.

item.title: Hypothesis-driven multi-objective optimization of the Belousov–Zhabotinsky reaction
item.description: Self-driving laboratories can optimize experiments, but whether they can reason scientifically about what to test remains unclear. Bayesian optimization (BO) provides uncertainty-aware search without explicit scientific interpretation, whereas language-model agents can formulate hypotheses but lack calibrated uncertainty. Here we introduce maLLaMar, which combines these capabilities in a physical self-driving laboratory. Using the Belousov–Zhabotinsky reaction, we compare BO-only, agent-led and cooperative experiment selection under matched experimental budgets. Agent-led selection raised the fraction of hour-long oscillations from 24% to 64%, while cooperation yielded the largest number of near-optimal conditions, eleven compared with two for either strategy alone. The best conditions sustained oscillations for the full hour with mean periods up to 4.7 times shorter than the highest-scoring literature formulation re-measured on our platform. Hypotheses recorded prospectively during experimentation were evaluated against an exhaustive 294-condition reference map that was never available to the agent. The map supported or refined several predictions and falsified generalizations drawn from sparsely sampled regions. Statistical optimization and explicit scientific reasoning thus contribute complementary capabilities, allowing an autonomous laboratory both to find improved conditions and to generate claims that independent experiments can test.

item.title: The Reverse Pourbaix Explorer: a condition-first screening tool of aqueous stability on the Materials Project
item.description: Aqueous stability is a critical constraint in the discovery of materials for electrocatalysis, corrosion-resistant systems, and electrochemical energy technologies. Conventional Pourbaix analysis follows a material-first workflow in which a predefined composition is evaluated across pH and electrochemical potential. Here, we introduce the Reverse Pourbaix Explorer, an interactive, condition-first screening application hosted on the Materials Project. This tool identifies structures predicted to be stable at user-selected aqueous operating conditions using a pre-computed dataset of Pourbaix decomposition energies evaluated across pH and potential. Users select an operating condition and stability tolerance from an interactive heatmap and retrieve a filterable list of candidate structures. The application further integrates adsorptionenergy data from the Open Catalyst Project, enabling candidates to be screened jointly according to aqueous stability and catalytic binding-energy descriptors. We demonstrate the application’s utility with two examples: stable, conductive materials under acidic OER conditions, and CO2 reduction candidates screened by stability, conductivity and adsorption energy. These examples show how the application can reduce a large materials database to tractable candidate sets while retaining direct links to the underlying structures, Pourbaix analyses and adsorption configurations for further scrutiny. However, the predictions remain limited by thermodynamic approximations. The Reverse Pourbaix Explorer application lowers the technical barrier to large-scale aqueous stability screening and provides an extensible platform for data-driven materials and catalyst discovery.

item.title: From Small-Data Conductivity Prediction to Bayesian Optimization of Electrolyte Formulations with a Tabular Foundation Model
item.description: We evaluate whether a frozen tabular foundation model, TabPFN, can use limited measurements to predict conductivity and guide electrolyte formulation search without explicit transport equations or task-specific physics-constrained training. On the AMPERE conductivity dataset, 40 labeled context samples yield a mean absolute percentage error (MAPE) of 5.56% on 60 held-out measurements, close to the 5.32% reported for the original physics-augmented AMPERE model and below the conventional regression baselines under locally matched conditions. Additional evaluations on CALiSol-23, Flores, ionic-liquid, and polymer-electrolyte datasets support broader predictive applicability, while target-domain measurements improve shifted-domain predictions through context updates alone. The main Bayesian optimization application revisits the AMPERE rate-performance search setting: TabPFN-predicted conductivity and operating salt concentration form a two-dimensional representation for a separate Gaussian process (GP) surrogate. Across two temperatures, measured-pool replays require 13.90 evaluations on average to find the best measured formulation, reducing cost by 45.6% relative to random search and 9.1% relative to composition inputs. Two further applications examine TabPFN as a direct objective surrogate. In sequential Clio conductivity replay, a fixed acquisition rule requires 11.5 evaluations on ten new starts, 38.2% fewer than random search and close to independently selected GP (11.0). In the ionic-polymer study, seven initial measurements support ranking the source study's recommended formulation at 21–27 among 497 candidates, versus 44 for Gaussian process regression. Together, these cases show how context-based prediction can support candidate selection through property-informed representations and direct objective surrogates.

item.title: Automating the Evaluation of Diffusion Coefficients from GITT Experiments using ”GITTcalc”
item.description: The galvanostatic intermittent titration technique (GITT) is a widely used method to evaluate the lithium diffusion coefficient in battery electrode materials. Here we introduce GITTcalc, an automatic analysis tool based on python for GITT experiments that extracts information about diffusion coefficients from raw data. It includes a graphical user interface (GUI) based on Tkinter and offers interoperability with OriginLab. The functionality and working principle of the program is demonstrated by an exemplary analysis of LiMn2O4 and LiNiO2 used as cathode materials for lithium-ion batteries. GITTcalc can be used by scientists with and without programming experience to facilitate the reproducible extraction of DLi from GITT data, with reliable error bars, and with sanity checks to identify if the fundamental GITT assumptions are respected.

item.title: Motion in Stillness: An Open-Source Python Toolkit for Visualizing Time-Dependent Hydrogen Wavefunctions
item.description: Orbital shapes and nodes are core learning objectives in chemistry and physics. Many tools can render a wavefunc- tion’s phase as a color map. Yet rendering it is not teaching it: students often cannot explain what phase means, nor where Ψ’s time dependence lies. Since the density |Ψ|2 of a stationary state is constant, many infer Ψ is static. The opposite is true. For a complex stationary state Ψ(t) = ψe−iEnt/ℏ, the phase argΨ = argψ −Ent/ℏ is time-dependent, advancing uniformly everywhere except at the nodes; because all points advance in step, phase differences remain fixed, and the nodal structure is unchanged. At a node (ψ = 0) the amplitude vanishes and the phase is undefined, changing abruptly across the nodal surface. Ψ’s time dependence thus resides in its phase, sharply distinguished at nodal and non-nodal points. We present Time-HWV, an open-source Python toolkit that decouples and animates the real part, imaginary part, and density in synchronized 2D cross-section and 3D views. Students observe the quadrature oscillation of Re[Ψ(t)] and Im[Ψ(t)] while confirming that |Ψ(t)|2 = |ψ|2 is invariant. Time-HWV offers 2D cross-sections (slices), 3D surface plots of those cross-sections (height fields), and interactive Plotly volume renderings in a lightweight NumPy/SciPy/Matplotlib package, with standalone executables requiring no programming environment. Code and manual are included as Supporting Information.

item.title: Ammonia combustion kinetic model optimization using elementary rate coefficient and global combustion data
item.description: Ammonia combustion kinetic models differ in key rate coefficients, and achieving consistent agreement with measurements across diverse conditions remains challenging. We optimize a detailed ammonia kinetic model derived from C3MechV4.0.1 for pure NH3, NH3/H2, and NH3/NO mixtures. The optimization uses direct rate determinations from 142 publications and 11,232 indirect combustion measurements from 113 publications, covering species concentrations, ignition delay times, laminar burning velocities, and extinction strain rates. Random-effects meta-analysis combines direct determinations into a prior distribution accounting for individual source uncertainties and additional disagreement between sources. General Bayesian inference updates this prior using a generalized likelihood based on the curve matching (CM) score, which quantifies agreement between model predictions and indirect measurements in values and trends. Neural network surrogates approximate these predictions for efficient likelihood evaluation. Sensitivity-based clustering partitions the indirect datasets into seven kinetic groups with characteristic chemistry. Networks sharing hidden layers within each group reduce mean surrogate curve error by 60 % relative to independent networks trained on the same data. Relative to the nominal model, the optimized model improves agreement in all seven kinetic groups and 71 % of individual datasets. Its overall weighted mean CM score exceeds those of all 54 published models evaluated. Optimization with the direct data-informed prior yields indirect data agreement comparable to that obtained with a uniform prior, while achieving substantially closer agreement with direct data. Chemical analysis links the improved predictions to underlying rate changes, while the posterior quantifies remaining rate uncertainties and identifies NH2 decomposition, H2NO chemistry, and N2Hx pathways as measurement priorities. The optimized ammonia chemistry is integrated into C3MechV4.2.0.

item.title: Development of a new isochromenylium-based derivatizing reagent for the analysis of α-amino acids and related compounds by LC-MS
item.description: A new pyrylium salt, 3,6,7-trimethoxyisochromenylium tetrafluoroborate (TriMIC), was developed for the derivatization of α-amino acids and other compounds with an NH2 group for use in LC-MS analysis. TriMIC was prepared using routine synthetic procedures from inexpensive raw materials. It has high reactivity, and derivatization of α-amino acids occurs under mild reaction conditions in an acetonitrile-methanol mixture. The efficiency of amino acid derivatization was evaluated using 10 amino acids.

item.title: Gold(I)-Catalyzed Intramolecular Addition of Pyridines to Unactivated Alkenes: Synthesis of Indolizinium and Quinolinium Derivatives.
item.description: Nitrogen-containing heterocycles, such as indoliziniums and quinoliniums, are essential structural scaffolds in medicinal chemistry and include bioactive alkaloids of therapeutic interest. Herein, we report a regioselective gold(I)-catalyzed intramolecular cyclization enabling the addition of pyridine and quinoline motifs onto unactivated alkenes to form indolizinium and quinolinium derivatives in high yields, by using HFIP as the solvent and para-toluenesulfonic acid as an acidic additive. Over thirty derivatives were synthesized, with yields ranging from 43% to 97%, covering a wide diversity of substitutions on the pyridine ring, the alkene chain, and their linker. Extension of this strategy to an oxidant-free gold(I/III) redox cross-coupling further enabled direct aryl functionalization. Finally, the synthetic potential of these compounds was demonstrated through various post-functionalizations and a formal synthesis of gephyrotoxin, highlighting their value for drug discovery and natural product synthesis.

item.title: A knowledge-aware, constraint-guaranteed decoder for cyclic peptides
item.description: Cyclic peptides reach a prized middle ground between small molecules and biologics: large enough to grip the flat protein–protein interfaces that defeat conventional drugs, yet sometimes lipophilic enough to be taken as a pill. Deep generative models have transformed small-molecule and protein design, but cyclic peptides are a harder frontier, with a design space of non-canonical residues, N-methylation, D-amino acids and macrocyclic rings that is far too large to search by hand. The models built for it are also hard to evaluate: they are often scored by distribution metrics, judged by the predictor that trained them, or compared with untuned baselines at unequal budgets — tests on which a weak method can look strong. Here we present IH-LM, a cyclic-peptide generator that compiles the design rules directly into the decoder, so every molecule it completes satisfies them by construction; across a 900-molecule test set it also discarded no rule-satisfying string. The preliminary experimental results are promising. Benchmarked against tuned baselines at a matched sampling budget, it produces about three times as many valid, novel molecules as enumerating a monomer library (773 versus 246 per 1,000 samples) and spans about three times as many distinct scaffolds for the same effort. Because validity is guaranteed rather than scored, the full strength of evaluation can be devoted to the properties that decide a candidate’s fate — chemical diversity, permeability and, ultimately, target activity — which is where real progress in cyclic-peptide design will be won.

item.title: Ultrafast Non-Förster Energy Transfer in a DNA-Templated Cy3-Cy5 Assembly
item.description: Controlling electronic coupling between chromophores is central to the design of photonic materials, yet energy transfer at sub nanometer donor-acceptor separations, where the point-dipole Förster approximation becomes unreliable, remains difficult to probe experimentally. Here, we use a doublestranded DNA scaffold to position a Cy3 donor and a Cy5 acceptor within a few ångströms of each other and characterize their energy transfer using steady-state and femtosecond transient absorption spectroscopy, microsecond molecular dynamics and umbrella-sampling simulations, and TDDFT-based transition-charge (TrESP) coupling calculations. Absorption changes consistent with H-type heterodimer formation accompany a near-unity (0.96) energy-transfer efficiency, while Cy3 signal depletes and Cy5 signal rises within the ~200 fs instrument response. Simulations show that the Cy3 and Cy5 are moderately-to-strongly coupled in the vast majority of the thermal ensemble, leading to energy transfer lifetimes shorter than 150 fs, consistent with transient absorption measurements. These results establish DNA scaffolds as programmable platforms for accessing non-Förster energy-transfer regimes.

item.title: Rapid, High-Yielding, and Broad-Scope Silicon-Noded Single-Atom Ligation Platform
item.description: The node–module logic underpins DNA, RNA, and metal–organic frameworks. In small-molecule synthesis, SuFEx and PFEx exploit sulfur or phosphorus as single‑atom nodes for 10 modular ligations but are largely confined to amine and phenol modules. Silicon‑based ligation would offer a viable alternative, as both alcohols and phenols can serve as reliable modules, yet it has lacked efficient and controllable platforms. Herein, we report a silicon-noded ligation platform using bis(2,4,6-trimethoxyphenyl)silanes (bis(TMP)silanes) as the ligation hubs, enabling rapid, high-yielding ligation of both alcohol and phenol modules with broad functional-group tolerance.

item.title: Scalable Amidation Reaction by Resonant Acoustic Mixing. Application to the multi-gram scale synthesis of marketed Agrochemicals
item.description: Industrial amide bond formation in agrochemical manufacture still relies on low-molecularweight chlorinating agents and dipolar aprotic solvents. Herein, five marketed SDHI fungicides, Fenfuram (1), Boscalid (2), Mepronil (3), Flutolanil (4) and Fluxapyroxad (5), were prepared by TCFH-mediated one-pot/two-step amidation across three mechanochemical platforms (VBM, PBM and LA-RAM). The optimal reaction environment proved platform-dependent: ball-milling favoured solid K2HPO4, whereas LA-RAM required liquid N-methylimidazole acting as both base and grinding liquid, and added grinding media (GA-RAM) lowered the yield through degradation of the activated acyl intermediate. LA-RAM was the most efficient and most readily scalable platform, delivering 1–5 in 67–99% yield on a 93 mmol scale (up to 34.9 g per batch, a 160-fold scale-up) at room temperature in 2.5 h at η ≤ 0.2 µL mg-1 of ethyl acetate, without re-optimisation. HR-PXRD and microED confirmed the crystalline forms for agrochemicals 2, 4 and 5, and gave the first structures of 1 and 3. DOZN™ 3.0 and CHEM21 assessments showed reduced waste, elimination of POCl3, oxalyl chloride, DMF and CH2Cl2, and PMI halved for 4 (24.5 vs 50.4).

item.title: Diversity of N-terminal Sequences of Aβ Peptides Governs TDMQ20-Mediated CuII Extraction Efficiency and Kinetics
item.description: Alzheimer’s disease (AD) is recognized as the most common form of dementia, with no curative therapies available. One of the current strategies towards an AD drug focuses on the development of copper-binding ligands capable of extracting CuII ions from β-amyloid (Aβ) peptides, among which TDMQ20 has attracted considerable attention. However, previous studies of TDMQ20 have focused primarily on its interaction with Aβ(1–x) peptides, with no consideration given to the molecular heterogeneity of Aβ species present in the AD brain. In this work, we investigated the impact of two biologically relevant N-terminal truncations (4-x) and (5-x) on the formation of the CuIITDMQ20 complex, guided by their known avidity to bind CuII ions. These sequences were represented by water-soluble-(non-aggregating) Aβ(4–16) and Aβ(5–16) peptides. We also reevaluated the CuII-binding properties of TDMQ20 and its interaction with the standard CuIIAβ(1–16) complex. Using stopped-flow kinetics, we confirmed the immediate and complete extraction of CuII ion from CuIIAβ(1–16) complex in the presence of equimolar TDMQ20. Importantly, however, CuIIAβ(4–16) and CuIIAβ(5–16) exhibited marked resistance to TDMQ20-mediated demetallation, revealing strong dependence of CuII extraction on the Aβ sequence. These findings suggest that the heterogeneity of Aβ species in AD-affected brains can be an important factor determining the efficacy of CuII-targeting therapeutic strategies.

item.title: Visible light-driven amide bond formation between carboxylic acids and amines
item.description: The direct formation of amide bonds from carboxylic acids and amines remains challenging due to rapid acid–base neutralisation, which necessitates prior activation of one or both substrates. Here, we report a visible-light-mediated strategy for direct amide coupling using a combination of thiocyanate and Rose Bengal. The reaction proceeds under mild conditions, without the need for anhydrous solvents or an inert atmosphere, and produces amides in moderate yields from a range of aromatic or aliphatic carboxylic acids and α-hydrogen-bearing amines. Control experiments showed that molecular oxygen is required for the reaction, in addition to ammonium thiocyanate. Substrate scope investigation revealed tolerance to both aromatic and aliphatic substituents on both the carboxylic acid and the amine. Notably, substrates bearing stereogenic centres, including amino acids, underwent coupling without detectable racemisation. This work introduces an alternative redox-mediated activation strategy that directly couples carboxylic acids and amines, complementing existing amide bond preparation methods.

item.title: Fine-Tuning a Graph-Transformer ADMET Model Improves Half-Life and Plasma Protein Binding Concordance
item.description: Absorption, distribution, metabolism, excretion, and toxicity (ADMET) models are usually judged on predefined benchmark splits. Those splits are useful, but they do not show whether a model reproduces the pharmacokinetic (PK) numbers that are actually reported for individual drugs. Here we compared ADMET-AI with a fine-tuned NV-KERMT-70M-v2 model (“KERMT”) on the same Therapeutics Data Commons (TDC)-aligned endpoint definitions. KERMT was fine-tuned in two stages: a protocol check on the ChEMBL multitask (ChEMBL-MT) data set, then TDC-aligned regression and classification fine-tuning on merged ChEMBL, Biogen, ExpansionRx/OpenADMET and TDC data. Two retrospective literature comparisons were run. The first used a curated 25-drug oncology panel: for half-life (n = 17) KERMT cut mean absolute error (MAE) from 46.81 to 16.83 h (paired Wilcoxon p = 0.0046, Holm-adjusted p = 0.0139, closer for 13 of 17 drugs); volume of distribution at steady state (VDss, n = 12) and hepatocyte clearance (n = 17) showed no statistically supported difference. The second, reported here for the first time, is an expanded three-way comparison of 53 oncology drugs × 3 endpoints (159 drug-endpoint rows) against curated literature and label values. On the 48 drugs with a usable half-life reference, KERMT more than halved the error (MAE 19.43 vs 43.38 h; median absolute error 12.01 vs 35.30 h; geometric mean fold error, GMFE, 2.72 vs 3.69; within 2-fold 41.0% vs 25.0%), was closer for 34 of 48 drugs (70.8%; 95% confidence interval, CI, 55.9-83.0%), and the paired Wilcoxon test was significant (p = 0.0002; Holm-adjusted p = 0.0004). The advantage persisted after each model's systematic bias was removed (p = 0.0004), so it is not a simple scale offset: ADMET-AI over-predicted half-life for 35 of 48 drugs (mean bias +29.20 h) whereas KERMT was mildly conservative (-13.79 h). For plasma protein binding ratio (PPBR, n = 21) KERMT had lower MAE (7.05 vs 9.44 percentage points) and the only statistically significant rank agreement with literature seen anywhere in this study (Spearman ρ = 0.540, p = 0.012, vs 0.400, p = 0.073), but the paired error difference was not significant (p = 0.157). One endpoint failed outright and we state it plainly: KERMT VDss predictions collapsed to near-baseline behaviour. They occupied a narrow band (46 of 53 drugs between 0 and 10 L/kg; standard deviation 3.64 vs 6.71 L/kg for ADMET-AI), no drug in the panel had an assay-matched VDss reference, and on the six drugs with an approximate reference the per-drug KERMT predictions (MAE 2.18 L/kg) were no better than replacing the entire model with one constant (MAE 2.14 L/kg) and worse than a no-information baseline (1.71 L/kg). KERMT VDss output should therefore not be used. A deliberately strict control bounds the positive findings as well: against a structure-blind constant predictor built by leave-one-out from the reference values, KERMT was statistically indistinguishable on both endpoints (half-life MAE 19.43 vs 16.07 h, p = 0.051; PPBR 7.05 vs 7.24 percentage points, p = 0.812), while ADMET-AI was significantly worse than that constant for half-life (p < 0.0001). We therefore make no claim of accurate numerical point prediction; the supported claims are that fine-tuning removes ADMET-AI's large systematic half-life error and that the PPBR rank correlation is compound-specific signal a constant cannot possess. Physically impossible values occurred in 16 of 159 KERMT rows and 21 of 159 ADMET-AI rows. Across 30 classification endpoints, mean inter-model Pearson correlation was 0.711 and mean binary agreement at 0.5 was 89%, which measures similarity, not accuracy. This version does not yet include official Therapeutics Data Commons benchmark-group evaluation of the fine-tuned models, replicate training seeds, or a training-set overlap audit; those gaps are declared explicitly rather than left implicit. The overall conclusion is endpoint-specific: fine-tuned KERMT is a materially better-calibrated half-life and plasma-protein-binding predictor than ADMET-AI on this panel, it is not yet a demonstrated ranking model for half-life, and its VDss head is unusable.

item.title: In-silico investigation of small molecule inhibitors of malaria-inducing cycloguanil-resistant Plasmodium falciparum dihydrofolate reductase
item.description: Plasmodium falciparum dihydrofolate reductase (DHFR) is the target of antimalarial drugs such as cycloguanil. However, mutations of DHFR, particularly the A16V and S108T variants, induce steric interactions that confer resistance to cycloguanil. It is crucial to find new therapeutics to combat cycloguanil-resistant strains of P. falciparum. We used in-silico methods to investigate possible drug candidates of A16V+S108T DHFR, a key cycloguanil-resistant double mutant. Using a large chemical library, we performed structure-based virtual screening to discover novel small molecule inhibitors of mutant DHFR. Molecular dynamics simulations show that the top-ranked compound from virtual screening, ligand 4, retains a stable binding pose. MM-GBSA calculations rank ligand 4 above cycloguanil and three other known DHFR inhibitors. Through these simulations, we identify a small molecule compound possessing more favorable binding free energies to DHFR than those of cycloguanil.

item.title: Photoluminescent Ratiometric and Lifetime Thermometry Governed by Water Dynamics in Heterometallic M(s-block)-Ce(III) Tricyanomethanide-Based Coordination Polymers
item.description: It is important to develop novel optical materials combining effective photoluminescence (PL) with a highly sensitive optical response to external stimuli. Cerium(III) complexes, whose efficient luminescence, ascribable to the d-f electronic transitions, is modulated by the coordination environment, are promising in this context. Here, experimental and theoretical studies on achieving the combination of a high room-temperature (RT) visible emission quantum yield (QY) of up to 0.94 (370 nm excitation) with the ratiometric optical thermometry of a relative thermal sensitivity reaching 9.2% K−1 above RT are reported. This was realized by linking Ce(III) centers with anionic tricyanomethanide ligands and s-block metal ions into rigid coordination polymers of the general formula of {AICeIII[C(CN)3]4(H2O)} (ACe, A = Na, K, Rb). They exhibit blue PL of dual ligand–Ce(III) origin, with the chromaticity and QY tuned by alkali metals. Moreover, they reveal strong temperature dependence of optical characteristics, including PL lifetime, which was correlated with thermally activated vibrations of coordinated aqua ligands, as was depicted by the H-to-D exchange and distinct dielectric relaxation processes. This water dynamics influencing PL was utilized for optical sensing of temperature, which was explored through ratiometric and lifetime-based approaches with particularly good performance in the around-and-above RT region.

item.title: pKasso: Accurate and accessible prediction of small-molecule protonation states
item.description: The protonation states of molecules are tightly linked to their physicochemical properties. Accurately predicting protonation states is therefore important for applications such as docking-based virtual screening in drug discovery. Modern machine-learning models can predict molecular pKa values with good accuracy, but obtaining pH-dependent protonation-state ensembles from available open-source models can cause substantial installation and workflow overhead. Commercial tools provide convenient alternatives but can entail substantial licensing costs. We here present pKasso, an accurate, fast, accessible, extensible, and easy-to-use open-source package to compute pH-dependent protonation-state ensembles of small molecules. pKasso enumerates relevant protonation microstates, integrates the existing pKa-prediction models MolGpKa and Uni-pKa, and converts their predictions into microstate populations and macroscopic pKa values. In addition, pKasso can combine predictions from multiple pKa-prediction models and report their disagreement as a qualitative indicator of predictive uncertainty. We evaluate pKasso on six benchmark datasets, where it achieves prediction accuracy competitive with state-of-the-art models. pKasso supports single-molecule and batch workflows. It is available as a web server (tools.bindresearch.org/pkasso), a Python library (pip install pkasso), and a command-line interface (github.com/bindresearch/pkasso).

item.title: When Can a Molecular-Dynamics Simulation Stop?
item.description: Molecular-dynamics (MD) simulations are usually run for a prespecified duration, even when the goal is to estimate an equilibrium observable to a stated precision. Stopping as soon as an estimated uncertainty becomes small enough is attractive, but repeated inspection invalidates uncertainty statements calibrated for a fixed time. We formulate data-dependent stopping as an inferential problem with an explicit precision target and a simultaneous-in-time coverage requirement, and organise it into four gated stages: temporal prediction against strong baselines, uncertainty calibration, an anytime-valid stopping rule, and measured high-performancecomputing (HPC) savings. We report exploratory first-stage results on four incrementally assembled ATLAS cohorts, using sequence-grouped cross-validation and a target computed only from frames after a 20 ns prefix. In the largest cohort (757 systems, 1,243 replicas, 689 sequence groups), ridge regression on 48 prefix summaries and a residual gated recurrent unit (GRU) both reduced RMSD mean absolute error relative to last-value persistence (0.610 and 0.636 versus 0.673 Å; paired bootstrap intervals excluding zero), whereas the GRU–ridge difference was not significant in any cohort. A genuine structure-only baseline, a compatible mdCATH analysis, sequential coverage and HPC cost measurements are still outstanding, so no stopping policy or computational saving is claimed.

item.title: Mixed-Valence Chemistry without Fractional Electrons in Variational 2-Electron Reduced Density Matrix Theory via Local Integer-Charge Constraints
item.description: The tractable capture of strong, or multi-reference correlation effects continues to present a formidable challenge at the forefront of quantum chemistry. Variational two-electron reduced density matrix (v2RDM) theory presents a polynomially scaling approach to multi-reference calculations, but its use of approximate N-representability conditions yields lower bounds to the true energy and possibly unphysical descriptions. We demonstrate that in mixed-valence transition-metal clusters ([Fe2S2], [Fe3S4], [Co2S2], [Ni2S2]) the common 2-and 3-particle N-representability conditions allow for charge-delocalization error, which affects the ability of v2RDM to both qualitatively and quantitatively describe their properties and redox chemistry, as redox-active electrons may be spuriously spread over multiple metal centers. Here, we introduce local integer-charge constraints that enforce the exact lower bound on the charge variance of metal-centered orbital subspaces and which may be imposed at minimal additional cost. We demonstrate that these constraints remove 22 to 89% of the energy error and 52 to 95% of the error in the metal d-electron populations, resulting in significant improvements to calculated ionization energies.

item.title: Unlocking the promise of materials AI through application proxies and protected collaboration
item.description: AI-guided and robotic laboratories can accelerate experiments within a company, but materials development still depends on repeated testing across company boundaries. Here we show in controlled simulation how investment in application-relevant private testing reduces that external work. We extend Minimum Knowledge Collaboration with application proxies, calling the extension MKC2. Suppliers develop combinations of physical tests and reference assemblies that capture how their materials respond under relevant product conditions. They train private models on the resulting curves and features, and the product integrator calibrates joint predictions against complete-product tests. Bidirectional MKC messages connect private material selection to the product requirements while raw curves and model parameters remain local. In sixteen paired two-company programs, 72 additional private training curves per program accompany a 93% reduction in subsequent product testing at a target of 90% of the best available combination. Target attainment rises from twelve to all sixteen programs within the fixed test horizon. Including the shared initial product campaign gives a 39% reduction. Matched two- and four-company studies and a reference-training sensitivity study examine the same exchange under prescribed physical response families. The benefit depends on developing informative tests, training useful predictions and acting on them in collaboration. AI and robotics can make the private investment faster. MKC2 connects that application learning to fewer tests across company boundaries.

item.title: Inhibiting LINE-1 retrotransposons therapeutically in disease
item.description: The LINE-1 retrotransposon is a virus-like genomic element that can activate in diseased cells. It has been implicated in cancer, autoimmunity, developmental disorders, infectious disease and neurodegeneration. LINE-1 can be inhibited by reverse transcriptase inhibitors, small molecules originally developed for HIV. The correlation between HIV and LINE-1 inhibition is ∼0.9 on a log scale, in spite of >450 Mya of evolutionary history since retroviruses diverged from retrotransposons. Suppression of HIV requires prevention of a completed 9.7 kb virus insertion into the genome in immune cells. However, every cell in the body already contains >100 copies of LINE-1 that can potentially activate. Even incomplete LINE-1 mediated insertions can cause damaging mutations and genome instability. Furthermore, partial HIV and LINE-1 products in the cytoplasm of cells can contribute to an inflammatory immune response. Preclinical studies have shown LINE-1 inhibitors slow the progression of otherwise unrelated diseases. LINE-1’s contribution to these diseases can potentially be quantified using single-nucleus whole-genome sequencing on diseased tissue, enabling prioritization of disease selection for therapeutic development. Furthermore, LINE-1’s ORF1p protein can be measured in the blood of individuals with certain cancers. LINE-1 inhibitors could therefore be extended to various diseases. Potentially used both as an anti-inflammatory and prophylactically to help preserve genome integrity. Reverse transcriptase inhibitors are available at low cost for HIV, and higher doses of some could be used to inhibit LINE-1. However, reverse transcriptase inhibitors do not prevent DNA cutting by LINE-1’s endonuclease. Novel inhibitors may therefore be required. This, combined with novel diagnostics opens up possibilities for inhibiting LINE-1 therapeutically in disease

item.title: A Graphene Oxide–Coco Pith Fiber–Polyvinyl Alcohol Non-Structural Composite Filter for Lead [Pb(II)] Removal from Aqueous Solution: A Proof-of-Concept Study
item.description: Lead [Pb(II)] in drinking water is a persistent health risk, and low-cost filter media are of interest where centralised treatment is limited. This preliminary proof-of-concept study prepared a filter body from graphene oxide (GO), coco pith fiber and boric-acid-treated polyvinyl alcohol (PVA) and tested it once with a nominal 50 mg/L Pb(II) solution under gravity filtration. GO was made by a modified Hummers' method and examined by FTIR only; the composite itself was not characterized. The filtrate was analyzed by flame atomic absorption spectroscopy. The retained reading (0.0054 absorbance units) equalled the reagent blank and lay below the lowest calibration standard (5 mg/L), giving an apparent residual of 0.53 mg/L (apparent removal 98.9%). Because this is at the blank level, the residual could not be quantified; the data support only a residual below 5 mg/L (removal above 90%). Filtered volume, flow rate and pH were not recorded, and no controls, adsorption-parameter studies, replicates or reusability tests were performed. The results are indicative only and define the experiments needed to assess this material.

item.title: Coupled Condensation–Melting Heat Transfer and Thermal Design Limits of a Steam-Assisted Pipeline Cleaning Crawler: A Probabilistic Modeling Study
item.description: Steam-assisted pipeline cleaning couples condensation heat transfer, melting of a deposit and a thermally protected tool, and the coupling, not any single component, sets its limits. We study a motorized steam-assisted crawler with a probabilistic model: transient conduction through an aluminum–aerogel–titanium wall into a lumped battery pack, film condensation, a melt model with a retained liquid film whose resistance is the dimensionless group Pif=hs/kl, a dynamic film balancing melt production and gravity drainage, an orifice model of the bypass relief, and a steam budget. The conduction and melt formulas are benchmarked against an independent solver 2 and the Neumann solution; no experiment was available for the coupled model. Under assumed input distributions, with 40 mm of aerogel the pack stays at or below 55 °C for 45 min in 98.9% of draws at 25 °C but 22% at 45 °C. The median range per deployment is 138 m if molten deposit leaves at once, 18 m with the dynamic film (0.35 mm) and 2 m with none removed; Sobol indices attribute 55% of the range variance to the film. The condensation correlation changes the instant-removal range by 25%, a Class 150 steam limit of 195 °C by 3%. A 1 km line needs a median of 57 deployments with the dynamic film (8 with instant removal), and the hull does not fit pipes below 8 in. These are model probabilities, not field reliabilities.

item.title: Pairing manure and lignocellulosic biochars to reduce phosphorus losses from manure fertilisers
item.description: Manures supply less nitrogen relative to phosphorus than crops require, so applying them to meet N demand accumulates P in soils and increases losses to water. Pyrolysis reduces the solubility of manure P, but the fraction that remains soluble is still vulnerable to runoff. This study tested whether lignocellulosic biochars applied alongside manure biochars can recapture that fraction. Poultry litter and dairy slurry were pyrolysed at 300, 500, and 700 °C, and their release of phosphate, ammonium, and nitrate was measured in 30-day batch incubations and in packed beds. Their leachates were incubated for 28 days with cocoa pod and coconut shell biochars produced at the same temperatures. Pyrolysis reduced soluble N release to at most 0.57 mg N/g, and phosphate release fell with peak temperature. Recapture by high-ash cocoa pod biochars rose with peak temperature, while low-ash coconut shell biochars released more phosphate to the leachate as temperature rose. Only cocoa pod biochar produced at 700 °C recaptured net phosphate, removing 0.71 mg P/g from poultry litter biochar leachate, most likely by precipitation, and neither lignocellulosic biochar captured substantial nitrate. A working system must combine a low-temperature manure biochar with a high-temperature, high-ash lignocellulosic biochar, here at a mass ratio of approximately 4:1 for a total application rate of 5 t/ha for winter wheat, costing 30–76 times more than mineral P fertiliser. The strategy’s added value lies in reducing nutrient losses and pollution, alongside biochar’s sterility, sustainability, and contribution to nutrient use efficiency via moisture and microbial communities.

item.title: Self-Assembled Chiral Lipid Phases for Passive RNA Capture
item.description: Sealed lipid vesicles provide useful models for compartmentalization, but their bilayer boundaries limit post-assembly uptake of hydrated macromolecules such as RNA. Here, we demonstrate that short-chain monoacylglycerides form assemblies that take up RNA. Glycerol monodecanoate (GMD) and glycerol monononanoate (GMN) spontaneously organize in water into sponge phases (L3) with interconnected aqueous channels. RNA uptake into these preformed assemblies is accompanied by restructuring toward vesicular morphologies, suggesting a pathway in which RNA enters through open aqueous channels and becomes retained during and after membrane reorganization. GMD assemblies preferentially retain RNA oligonucleotides over the mononucleotide adenosine monophosphate (AMP). Crucially, lipid stereochemistry (R, S and rac) differentially affects the response of the sponge assemblies to RNA, with R-GMD maintaining higher RNA association over time in comparison to S- and rac-GMD. These findings show how molecular chirality can propagate into self-assembled noncovalent systems providing selectivity for RNA retention.

item.title: Intrinsic and Extrinsic Factors Governing CO Electro-Oxidation Pathways at Low Potentials on Platinum Single Crystal Electrodes
item.description: CO electro-oxidation on Pt is often interpreted primarily in terms of surface structure and CO coverage, yet the origin of the electro-oxidation processes preceding the main stripping peak remains unresolved. Here, we show that CO pre-oxidation is governed by the coupled effects of Pt surface structure, CO adlayer preparation, and the evolving electrostatic state of the Pt/CO-electrolyte interface. Using Pt single-crystal electrodes spanning the stereographic triangle and different CO adlayer preparation protocols, we demonstrate that long-range structural order in the Pt substrate is the only common structural requirement identified for CO pre-oxidation. The specific conditions under which the process occurs, however, depend strongly on surface orientation. Under potential-controlled CO adsorption, dissolved CO is required for pre-oxidation on Pt(111)-type surfaces but not on Pt(100)-type surfaces. Surface defects do not universally promote pre-oxidation: they inhibit pre-oxidation on Pt(100)-type surfaces and enhance it only on Pt(111)-type surfaces for specific terrace-step configurations when CO is adsorbed at sufficiently low potentials. Their principal role is therefore to modify the reactivity of neighboring terrace domains rather than to act as general active centers. On Pt(111)-type surfaces, the regions made electrochemically accessible during pre-oxidation correspond to extended (111) terraces. Partial electro-oxidation of the CO adlayer also induces structure-dependent relaxation of the remaining adlayer. Most importantly, stepwise CO stripping reveals contrasting coverage-dependent kinetic responses for CO pre-oxidation and the main oxidation process. We attribute this kinetic decoupling to competition between the positive feedback associated with the creation of vacant Pt sites and an opposing electrostatic constraint imposed by the negatively charged CO-covered interface, which likely limits the formation of reactive water-derived species required for CO electro-oxidation. The resulting picture identifies CO pre-oxidation as a collective interfacial phenomenon in which surface structure, adlayer organization, and interfacial electrostatics evolve together as CO is consumed.

item.title: Molecular Design of Non-Fluorinated Aryl-Extended Carbazole-Based Polymeric Membranes for Anion Exchange and Bipolar Membrane Water Electrolysis
item.description: The development of durable anion-exchange membranes (AEMs) that combine rapid hydroxide transport with restrained hydration and dimensional stability remains a central challenge for alkaline electrochemical technologies. Here, we synthesize a series of ether-free, arylexpanded carbazole-based AEMs bearing systematically varied N-alkyl substituents: N-ethyl (HCz-Et), N-butyl (HCz-Bu), and N-hexyl (HCz-Hex). This systematic modification allows us to investigate how N-alkyl substitution within a common aromatic framework affects the physical, chemical, and mechanical properties of the resulting AEMs. Within this aryl-expanded series, increasing the N-alkyl chain length progressively suppressed water uptake and dimensional expansion while maintaining high hydroxide conductivity at elevated temperature. Specifically, HCz-Hex exhibited a water uptake of 18.7% and swelling ratio of 4.2%, with an OH− conductivity of 178mS cm−1 at 80 ◦C, indicating that this architecture can sustain efficient ion transport with limited membrane swelling. Furthermore, HCz-Hex retained ≈ 91% of its initial ion-exchange capacity (IEC) after 1000 h in 1M KOH at 80 ◦C. This balance of hydration control, conductivity, and alkaline stability translates directly to device performance: HCz-Hex reaches ≈ 2.05V at 2.0A cm−2 in pure-water-fed AEM electrolysis at 70 ◦C and 6A cm−2 at ≈ 2.19V in 1M KOH at 55 ◦C, while sustaining operation at 1.0A cm−2 for ≈ 1000 h. Beyond AEM electrolysis, coupling HCz-Hex with the non-fluorinated cation-exchange polymer SPEEK produces a fully non-fluorinated, Nafion-free bipolar membrane (BPM), enabling BPM water electrolysis at ≈ 2.03V at 1.0A cm−2 with a reported water-dissociation overpotential of approximately 80mV. This study provides a basis for designing non-fluorinated AEMs with tailored membrane properties for high-performance AEM and BPM electrolysis.

item.title: TEBench: a source-labelled thermoelectric data collection with leakage-safe splits and baselines for machine learning
item.description: Machine-learning thermoelectric scores are difficult to compare when source provenance and split groups differ. TEBench organises Starrydata Experiment-labelled curves (30,530 samples, 1,648,315 points, 6,045 papers), a JARVIS-DFT extract (23,558 structures) and an audited bulk Bi2Te3 workbook (740 records, 151 DOIs) as separate domains. DFT and experiment are never pooled. Canonical composition keys, paper/family/formula grouping and an eight-paper own-data hold-out support leakage review. The original Bi2Te3 Seebeck random forest reaches test R2 = 0.935 but own-paper R2 = −1.21. A κ-specific physical screening rule retains 257,647 Starrydata points before composition parsing and split joining; the rerun gives test R2 = 0.045 (random forest) and 0.232 (gradient boosting). Validation-selected CPU gradient boosting and structure-derived JARVIS tabular features are evaluated beside preserved random-forest references. Composition-to-JID candidate matches are explicitly distinguished from unique structure identity. Extract hashes and transport-unit limitations are documented. These are proposed tasks and transparent baseline comparisons, not a released benchmark or a claim of state-of-the-art prediction.

item.title: Aromaticity, Electron Delocalization and Pauli Repulsion Explain Singlet and Triplet Energies in π-Systems Containing the Amide Moiety
item.description: Aromaticity has proven an invaluable principle for designing molecular singlet-fission chromophores. However, to effectively leverage aromaticity as part of a series of rational design principles, it is important to understand the interplay between aromaticity, electron delocalization, and singlet and triplet state energies. Here we report a multi-dimensional analysis of the relationship between aromaticity, electron-delocalization, and singlet/triplet state energies in a series of 114 amide-containing π-conjugated fused-ring systems. We show that E(S1) largely depends on the size of the π-system and the local (anti)aromatic character of each of its constituent rings. However, across the entire dataset, calculated E(T1) is less clearly correlated with any of our predictive metrics. In molecules with fewer than four linearly fused rings, E(T1) is correlated with the ground state’s IFDI (inter-fragment delocalization index), a measure of long-range electronic communication. In larger chromophores, this effect is less pronounced, reflecting the more delocalized triplet spin density and thus lower Pauli repulsion. We propose that the rational design of chromophores with narrow singlet-triplet gaps based on aromaticity rules should aim to tune E(S1) using π-system size and local (anti)aromaticity, and E(T1) by manipulating triplet aromaticity to minimize Pauli repulsion. [190/200]

item.title: GauMon: A Standalone, Cycle-Resolved Monitor for Gaussian Electronic-Structure Calculations
item.description: Electronic structure calculations can produce large and complex log files. Information such as self-consistent field (SCF) convergence, geometry optimization, numerical algorithms, and irregular termination can be found throughout the calculation. GauMon ( https://github.com/devashishdas/GauMon ) is an open-source Python desktop GUI application that monitors Gaussian calculation logs in real-time or allows examination of an existing log file. The software parses log files incrementally to monitor the state of a calculation. Features include numerical summaries, measurements of geometry change, Gaussian links, diagnostics based on the source of failure, and the option for a per-cycle breakdown. Separate windows for each type of calculation allow SCF cycles, quadratic-convergence linear-equation sub-calculations, and harmonic vibration analysis to be monitored. The software can launch a Gaussian executable and attach to the process. It can also be attached to existing or previous calculation processes in a read-only fashion. The Qt native GUI and PyQtGraph plotting require no browser or GPU. The code was tested with dummy input and output, regression testing, and three Gaussian logs provided. The parser was able to extract 19 SCF procedures from an optimization of a water cluster log, 19 incomplete SCF cycles from another calculation, and 5 linear solutions (4 converged and 1 incomplete) from the Fe-S example. This is just to confirm that the parser works and does not indicate any chemical accuracy or speed increases. GauMon provides a focused way to examine lengthy Gaussian calculations with clear indicators of uncertainties in the process, an estimate of the time remaining, and incomplete data.

item.title: Quantifying the Effectiveness of Independent Manual-Valve Verification in Preventing Product-Transfer Risks: A Monte Carlo Process-Safety Assessment
item.description: Manual valve line-ups before product transfers rely on rounds, radio confirmation and checklists, none of which observes valve position independently. We ask when an additional layer of temporary clamp-on position sensors on existing manual valves reduces transfer risk, and when alarm fatigue, bypass, common-cause failures and incomplete coverage remove the benefit. A Monte Carlo model of the line-up task, verified against closed-form results, an independent analytic model and automated tests, gave with assumed inputs for a 14-valve route an undetected-error probability per transfer of 4.03% with existing checks and 0.29% with direct 2 sensing and NFC identity (14-fold; sampling interval 13.6–14.3), assuming that operators always act on alarms. Varying 13 inputs gave a median reduction of 9.7 (5th–95th percentile 4.4–28); adding uncertain operator response, alarm fatigue and common-cause failures of the sensing layer gave 2.5 (0.9–4.8), with response the strongest driver. A mean response time of 10 min against 20 min available gave a factor of approximately 2. A factor of 10 required a response of at least 97%, bypass below 53% and common-cause probability below 2.3%. An illustrative event tree gave a 14-fold reduction in expected loss. Clustering of validations by valve cut the power of a 1000-validation pilot from 95% to 50%. Inputs, consequence probabilities and losses are assumed: the results are conditional, not credited risk reduction.

item.title: A Hidden Silver Oxide Layer Rewrites Molecular Fingerprinting in Surface-Enhanced Raman Spectroscopy
item.description: Gold (Au) and silver (Ag) are considered as interchangeable plasmonic components based on the implicit assumption that freshly prepared Ag nanomaterials remain metallic. However, we show, using in-situ surfaceaccessible SERS, that a sub-nanometer AgOx layer forms ubiquitously and instantaneously on colloidal Ag nanoparticles, and that this layer fundamentally alters our picture of how molecules interact with silver surfaces. Unlike the welldocumented long-term oxidation that slowly degrades Ag over weeks, this layer is an intrinsic property of a wide range of freshly prepared Ag nanomaterials and persists even in biological environments. This establishes the oxidationmodulated-adsorption (OMA) effect as a tunable parameter and rational basis for material selection in plasmonic technologies. We show that OMA can be quantified via the standard deviation of relative enhancement (𝜎𝑅𝐸) in SERS. Using SERS sensing as a representative application, we demonstrate that OMA causes the same molecule to yield distinct spectral fingerprints on Ag versus Au, and that harnessing OMA improves detection sensitivity by 500-fold, pushes clinically relevant concentrations into reach, and restores machine-learning classification from random chance to perfection. More generally, recognizing the OMA effect not only rewrites the underlying logic for designing plasmonic materials but also implies that the surface chemistry-related mechanisms in previously reported plasmonic technologies should be carefully re-examined.

item.title: Molecular thermal motion harvester for electricity conversion via contact electrification: Role and effect of design and additives
item.description: Converting the molecular thermal energy to electric energy via liquid-solid interfacial contact electrification was experimentally validated and it presents a promising approach towards a new type of green energy technology. In this work, nylon 66 and polystyrene layers coated on copper foils were employed as positive and negative electrodes, to investigate the effect of electrolytes, saccharides, and surfactants, as additives to water. This study aims to improve device performance and establish some basic design principles for molecular thermal energy conversion systems. Meanwhile, a series of experiments were carried out to investigate the influences of key structural components on the electric output of the device, intending to help refine the design concepts and to gain a better understanding of the working mechanisms. Our work revealed that the electric output of water was significantly enhanced after adding 5% Na2CO3. This study also attempts to develop new ideas to further enhance the electricity output of molecular thermal motion harvester.

item.title: BindCraft2 versus RFD4-Proteina for de novo peptide binder design against insecticide targets
item.description: De novo peptide binders are attractive leads for biological pesticides because they can be designed against validated insecticide targets without a small-molecule discovery campaign. Two generative pipelines dominate this space: BindCraft2, an AlphaFold2/ProteinMPNN campaign that accepts designs only after a cascade of structural filters, and RFD4-Proteina, a flow-matching foundation model that generates conditioned backbones and sequences in a single pass. We benchmarked both on three insecticide targets: acetylcholinesterase (PDB 1QON, 540 residues), the ecdysone receptor ligand-binding domain (1R1K, 236 residues) and the ryanodine receptor SPRY2 domain (6KIM, 169 residues). Every design was re-folded with the same AlphaFold2 oracle. RFD4 returned 300 designs in 3.3 GPU-hours, 82 of which passed a common re-folding screen. BindCraft2 returned 10 designs in 58.7 GPU-hours, none on two of the three targets, and 3 of its 10 passed the same screen. The advantage of RFD4 was entirely concentrated on the smallest, contiguous target: there it delivered 82 usable designs in 0.32 GPU-hours, against 3 in 1.95 GPU-hours from BindCraft2. On the two larger targets RFD4 complexes looked bound in the generated coordinates but did not survive re-folding, and BindCraft2 accepted nothing. Generation speed and re-foldable interface quality therefore separated on this target set: RFD4 is the more cost-effective generator, but neither method produced validated binders on two of the three targets.

item.title: Alchemical Free Energy Methods Reproduce Scaffold Modifications in a Macrocyclic Peptide PCSK9 Series
item.description: Free energy perturbation (FEP) methods are widely used in drug discovery campaigns to optimise the binding affinity of small molecule ligands. Recently, macrocyclic peptides have emerged as an increasingly attractive modality alongside small molecules and biologics. They possess the unique ability to bind to large, flat, and featureless binding sites that are inaccessible to small molecules, while offering a route to oral bioavailability, which antibodies lack. However, modelling macrocycles with FEP presents significant challenges. These campaigns frequently involve complex scaffold changes that extend beyond traditional R-group modifications and often utilise both canonical and non-canonical amino acids, necessitating specialised parameterisation protocols to handle this diverse chemical space. In this work, we address these challenges by benchmarking against the comprehensive structure activity campaign of Tucker et al. [1], which details the development of novel macrocyclic peptide inhibitors targeting PCSK9. We present open-source relative binding free energy (RBFE) protocols and methodological strategies for the range of transformations required by this series, spanning buried backbone N-methylation, olefin transformations, ring-breaking, and changes in net charge. Furthermore, we automatically parameterise these chemically diverse inhibitors using the OpenFF force fields and graph neural network partial charges. We compare three analysis protocols that differ in how equilibration and correlated sampling are treated, and report performance both edgewise and after maximum-likelihood estimation of absolute free energies. Under the most rigorous of these, in which equilibration is detected automatically, the campaign is recovered with an edgewise RMSE of 0.93 kcal mol−1 (95% CI 0.74–1.10 kcal mol−1). Reaching compound 35, the most potent compound considered here, requires five consecutive perturbations, each exercising a distinct modelling challenge and each falling well outside conventional R-group substitution. Every edge along this path is reproduced to within 1.39 kcal mol−1. Overall, this work broadens the applicability of FEP methods in drug discovery while also identifying their current limits.

item.title: Emergence of Atomic Energy States: Predicting Ionization Energies of One-Electron Systems via Nucleus-Driven Force Propagation in Real Space
item.description: Although probabilistic electron wave-function approaches provide solid mechanistic insights for molecules, their inherent reliance on static, boundary-dependent approximations limits the direct description of real-space molecular dynamics. This study demonstrates the emergence of highly accurate atomic energy states by a single nucleus-driven force-propagating framework within an open system.When compared withNIST ionization energy dataforone-electron systems,our model yields a 0.0000% relative error for the hydrogen atom (Z = 1), where the energy spectrum naturally emerges from the nucleus as wave maximum peaks in real space. Furthermore, by relying solely on the atomic number (Z) as an independent variable alongside fixed global parameters, the model autonomously generates macroscopic energy values across various elements,maintaining relative errors of less than 1% up to Pr (Z = 59) and remaining even for massive nuclei such as Au (1.88%) and Rn (2.59%), with relative errors quite low at 1.88% and 2.59%, respectively. These highly accurate predictions are achieved through the Causal Recording (CR) framework, which tracks the irreversible and continuous propagation of classical nuclear forces. Comparisons with the emergentLagrangianpathconfirmedthatmacroscopictrajectoriesandwavebehaviors autonomously emerge from the collective accumulation oflocalforce events.Ultimately,these results successfully confirm that intra-atomic electron behavior can be described by the classical force of the nucleus in real space.

item.title: Improving 13C Benchtop Hyperpolarization with TOTAPOL as a Polarizing Agent
item.description: Dissolution dynamic nuclear polarization (dDNP) offers a solution to the naturally low sensitivity of NMR spectroscopy thanks to signal enhancements by several orders of magnitude. However, this methodology usually requires high magnetic fields and cryogenic temperatures (typ. > 3 T and < 4.2 K), which implies complex and expensive experimental setups, usually hosted in dedicated facilities. In recent years, there has been a growing interest in more affordable and cost-effective systems, and our group has developed an approach based on a simple and affordable benchtop DNP polarizer. Mild experimental conditions (𝐵0 = 1 T and 𝑇 = 77 K) are applied, together with continuous microwave irradiation, to transfer the high electron spin polarization from TEMPOL to nuclear spins, achieving typically 100-fold signal enhancement on 1H nuclei in arbitrary samples. In the present study we aim at improving the NMR sensitivity of 13C nuclei at benchtop conditions by means of cross-polarization DNP (CP-DNP) using a dinitroxide polarizing agent (PA), TOTAPOL, and demonstrate that we can increase the 13C signal intensity by 50% compared to the use of TEMPOL. We rationalise the behaviour of the two PAs by analysing the interplay between 1H and 13C relaxation times during the CP contact time. Our study suggests that biradicals may offer a promising pathway to improve the 13C signal enhancement under CP-DNP at benchtop conditions.

item.title: From Individual Structure to Collective Topology: Cation Effects on the Hierarchical Organization of Interfacial Hydrogen Bond Networks
item.description: How electrolyte cations reshape the collective organization of interfacial water remains difficult to establish from local molecular descriptors. Here, we develop a graph-based hierarchical framework spanning molecular structure, network connectivity, and higher-order ring architecture, and apply it to molecular dynamics simulations of charged water/Pt(111) interfaces containing K+, Li+, and Ba2+. Molecular orientations respond primarily to surface charge, while molecular hydrogen bond statistics provide limited discrimination between Li+ and Ba2+. Collective descriptors reveal additional cation effects: hydrogen bond networks containing Ba2+ are more vulnerable than those containing Li+ to fragmentation upon removal of interfacial water molecules. Despite reduced connectivity with increasing surface charge magnitude and ion adsorption, more than 85% of interfacial water molecules remain in the largest connected component on average under all conditions studied. Four-and five-member rings dominate the interfacial networks, whereas increasing surface charge magnitude reduces the population of large rings and inter-ring connectivity. Connections involving large rings become less frequent from K+ to Li+ to Ba2+, revealing ion-dependent differences in ring organization. Larger rings preferentially involve water molecules with fewer hydrogen bonds, connecting higher-order architecture to local molecular environments.

item.title: High-resolution relaxometry suggests the presence of pervasive nano-second sugar motions in a DNA duplex.
item.description: Nucleic acids are central to many biomolecular processes central to cellular life, yet characterising their molecular motions and fluctuations with atomic resolution remains challenging. We introduce high-resolution relaxometry, combined with high-field nuclear spin relaxation, as a powerful tool to probe motions in nucleic acids. After recording an extensive spin-relaxation dataset from 2 to 23 T, we propose a framework, within the model-free approach, that allowed us to identify motions occurring both on the picosecond and low nanosecond time scales. By integrating these results with molecular dynamics simulations and ensembles, obtained from residual dipolar coupling (RDC) measurements, we propose a time-resolved model that includes fast helical motions and slower pervasive sugar puckering motions. The approach outlined in this study also provides a framework for interrogating molecular dynamics in nucleic acids with spin relaxation experiments and benchmarking molecular dynamics simulations that aim to characterise dynamic processes.

item.title: Unified Charge-Transfer Diagrams for Teaching Molecule-Surface Interactions
Optical Properties of Different Chemistries of Natural and Synthetic Melanin
item.description: Melanin, a ubiquitous black pigment, consists of at least five chemistries identified by the starting monomers involved in its polymerization. Natural melanin may also contain other components, such as lipids and proteins, that can affect its optical properties. Melanin is known for its high refractive index and broadband absorption. However, most optical-property observations are based on measurements of eumelanin-based chemistry. In this study, we used spectroscopic ellipsometry to measure the complex refractive index over a broad wavelength range (380–1700 nm) for the three main melanin chemistries: eumelanin, allomelanin, and pheomelanin. We compared the complex refractive indices of these materials with values obtained from UV absorption measurements, using an integrating sphere to minimize scattering effects. Our results show that melanin chemistry strongly influences optical properties. Pheomelanin from human red hair has the lowest absorption and refractive index, while poly(L-3,4-dihydroxyphenylalanine) (PDOPA; a polydopamine-based eumelanin chemistry) has the highest refractive index and absorption. We also observed variation in the optical properties of pheomelanin samples extracted from human red hair and rooster feathers. Thus, variations in melanin composition affect both the optical and thermal properties of melanin, highlighting the need to identify its precise chemistry in natural systems to understand melanin's impact on function and performance.

item.title: Multi-Criteria Decision-Making Framework for Sustainable Engineering Materials: Integrating Biopolymer Structure, Processing, Properties, Scalability, Techno-Economics, and Life-Cycle Assessment
item.description: Renewable biopolymers are often compared by feedstock origin, biodegradability, or isolated properties, yet an engineering decision concerns a biopolymer processed into a de-fined architecture for a specified application under practical manufacturing constraints. This study develops a multi-criteria decision-making framework for alginate, cellulose, lignin, chitosan, and starch in which the decision unit is a material–processing route–architecture–application system. Each unit is scored on molecular functionality, pro-cessing compatibility, architecture, application-relevant performance, and scalability, with independent evidence-confidence flags, explicit treatment of missing evidence, and bal-anced, performance-led, and manufacturability-led weighting scenarios. Techno-economic and life-cycle evidence is retained as a separate confidence and constraint layer. Fourteen decision units were evaluated from published literature across three contrasting demon-stration cases. Four units were classified as evidence-limited, converting data gaps into explicit research priorities. The framework provides a reproducible, transferable bridge between qualitative renewable-biopolymer reviews and application-specific materi-al-system design.

item.title: JAI: Physically Constrained Prediction of Conformer-Averaged Proton–Proton Coupling Constants in Solution
item.description: Machine-learning predictors of proton–proton coupling constants are usually trained on, and evaluated against, couplings computed for single geometries rather than the conformer-averaged values measured in solution. We describe JAI (J-coupling prediction with Artificial Intelligence), a graph transformer for 2J–5J(H,H) of small organic molecules trained on scaled Fermi-contact DFT couplings of about 3700 molecules, computed on geometries from the universal machine-learned potential UMA and averaged over conformers in six solvents, and on more than 25 000 curated experimental couplings annotated with their uncertainty, sign provenance and assignment. A fast mode predicts from the structure diagram; a conformer mode supplies, for each conformer of a reproducible search, the coefficients of Karplus-type expressions that are averaged with predicted populations; and a weighted combination of the two gives the final output, with 68 % and 90 % intervals calibrated on cross-validation errors. Against experimental couplings, the combined output reaches a mean absolute error of 0.43 Hz in cross-validation and 0.55 Hz when all compounds from the same literature source are held out together, our most realistic estimate for new chemistry.
