Here, we report a dual-microcapsule strategy that activates ultralong RTP through damage-triggered in situ polymerization. Two complementary types of microcapsules, separately encapsulating an epoxy precursor and an amine solution containing organic phosphors, were incorporated into a coating. Mechanical damage ruptured both microcapsules, allowing the released components to undergo localized polymerization and form a rigid cross-linked epoxy network that suppresses nonradiative deactivation of the phosphors and enables persistent RTP at the damaged region. Among the investigated luminogens, the amino-substituted phosphor exhibited the best performance, delivering an RTP lifetime of 1857 ms together with remarkable resistance to water, organic solvents, and extremely acidic and alkaline environments. The localized RTP activation enabled high-contrast visualization of scratches and compressive damage. Furthermore, the time-dependent organic afterglow was exploited to construct dynamic multilevel anti-counterfeiting patterns with programmable temporal information. This work establishes damage-triggered in situ polymerization as a general strategy for on-demand activation of organic RTP, providing a versatile platform for intelligent damage self-reporting, dynamic anti-counterfeiting, and advanced mechanoresponsive photonic materials.

item.title: A bespoke, token-efficient LLM inference pipeline for extracting polymer diffusion coefficients from scientific literature
item.description: Automated creation of actionable chemical datasets through large language model (LLM) interpretation of chemistry publications has become an engineering challenge rather than a frontier AI problem. We present Chemstractor, a bespoke extraction pipeline designed for use with open‑weight LLMs that can be executed locally on hardware typically available to university research environments. As a test case, the extraction techniques are applied to polymer diffusion coefficients, commonly used for the prediction of polymer molecular weights and for evaluating emerging universal calibration curves. The pipeline combines modern PDF parsing, table focused chunking, structured prompting, and an agent orchestrated calculator tool to handle mathematical transformations and reduce hallucinations. Chemstractor achieves strong performance, including a low hallucination rate, while maintaining extremely low token usage and requiring no paid API access. The methodology provides an accessible and efficient route to generating validated, analysis ready datasets and offers a template for extracting similarly complex scientific parameters in other domains.

item.title: Chemistry-informed non-covalent graphs and pharmacophore supervision for molecular property prediction
item.description: Graph neural networks describe a molecule by its covalent bonds, however, many molecular properties are shaped by contacts between atoms that are not bonded to each other. Existing models either ignore these non-covalent interactions or approximate them with a distance cutoff that cannot distinguish an interaction from mere proximity. Here we introduce a framework that injects chemical knowledge at two levels. First, intramolecular hydrogen bonds and van der Waals contacts become graph edges only when they satisfy interaction-specific topological and geometric criteria; these edges form a separate graph whose layer refines the atom states of a covalent encoder, and the two readouts are fused through a task-aware gate. Second, an auxiliary head supervises every atom with its pharmacophoric roles with expanded σ-hole interaction dictionary. We show that the rule-based graph is about twenty times sparser than a 5-Å cutoff graph, that the gated model reduces to a covalent model as its gate closes and adds a generalisation term bounded by a multiple of its maximal gate value, and that its predictions are Lipschitz in the atomic coordinates as long as the edge set is unchanged. On seven MoleculeNet classification benchmarks under scaffold splitting and without pretraining, ChemPrior-GAT achieves the best ROC-AUC on three benchmarks and the lowest average rank, and the same two modules also improve AttentiveFP, demonstrating that the proposed strategy is transferable to other GNN architecture. Pharmacophore-level attributions are consistent with established chemical principles. In prospective experimental validation involving 16 compounds, the model achieved a mean absolute error (MAE) of 0.50 log units between predicted and experimentally measured logD7.4 values.

item.title: Development and Evaluation of an Agentic Suite of Tasks Covering a Computational Chemistry Curriculum
item.description: Computational chemistry, increasingly enabled by high-performance computing, accelerates research across many areas of chemistry. However, heterogeneous software packages, input formats, and output conventions create a steep learning curve that also complicates simulation scripting and automation. Large language models (LLMs) can lower this barrier by helping users prepare calculations, execute workflows, and interpret results. We present ASSAY (Agentic Simulation Suite for Automated Chemistry), an open-source agentic toolkit for quantum chemistry designed for undergraduate CC education. To align ASSAY with current curricula, we analyzed syllabi from 17 courses at public and private universities in and outside the United States. ASSAY supports example-driven learning through input generation and output interpretation, while its local and remote workflows can introduce students to distributed computing, batch queues, and file management. In a benchmark spanning 12 skills and 8 LLMs, ASSAY achieved a mean pass rate of 94.04%, with six models achieving at least 98%. These results establish ASSAY as a reproducible, integrity-first foundation for making computational chemistry more accessible to students and reliable for researchers.

item.title: Assessing the predictive limits of machine learning on cyclic peptides
item.description: Machine learning (ML) has become a key tool in molecule discovery and optimization. Yet cyclic peptides, which occupy an intermediate chemical space between small molecules and proteins, have received limited attention in ML research, leaving the predictive value of current methods and future research needs unclear. To address this gap, we systematically evaluated ten model families (from classical ML approaches to pretrained deep-learning models) and nine molecular representations (from molecular descriptors to strings and graphs) across twelve prediction tasks spanning three properties and 9,341 peptides. Membrane permeability showed the clearest predictive signal, whereas binding-affinity and half-life prediction remained challenging. Evaluating models against explicit ‘no-skill’ references was central to interpreting these results and contextualizing performance across endpoints and data splits. No single model family performed best across all tasks: tree ensembles were strong in regression, while pretrained chemical language models performed best on average in classification. We further show that data splitting, task formulation, and dataset composition can influence apparent performance. Together, these findings highlight data availability and assay consistency, limited statistical power, and evaluation design as key challenges for cyclic-peptide modeling. To support progress in these areas, we release CycPepNet (https://github.com/molML/CycPepNet), an open framework that brings together curated datasets, evaluation protocols, and full results to enable reproducible comparisons and future method development.

item.title: Intracellular fate of structurally heterogeneous carbon nitride structures in mammalian cells
item.description: Carbon nitride materials are increasingly investigated for photocatalysis, environmental remediation, and emerging biomedical applications. Although the biological behavior of carbon nitride quantum dots has been studied quite extensively, interactions of larger and structurally heterogeneous carbon nitride structures with cells remain poorly understood. Here, we investigate the intracellular fate of two carbon nitride samples possessing markedly different characteristic dimensions, spanning a range from approximately 100 nm to several micrometers. Confocal microscopy and flow cytometry demonstrated pronounced concentration-and time-dependent cellular accumulation of both samples in HeLa cells. Pharmacological inhibition experiments indicated that uptake is largely mediated by actin-dependent phagocytosis. Super-resolution by optical reassignment imaging and transmission electron microscopy confirmed intracellular localization of carbon nitride structures within membranebound organelles. Live-cell imaging showed progressive accumulation of internalized carbon nitride structures within the lysosomal compartment, consistent with trafficking through the endolysosomal pathway. The larger carbon nitride structures exhibited greater intracellular persistence than their smaller counterparts. Despite efficient uptake, vesicular localization, intracellular processing, and prolonged retention, neither cell proliferation nor cellular stress pathways (interrogated through canonical markers for endoplasmic reticulum stress, oxidative stress, apoptosis, and DNA damage) showed substantial alterations after 12 hours under non-illuminated conditions. These findings demonstrate that structurally heterogeneous carbon nitride architectures remain biologically accessible across a broad size range and provide new insight into their intracellular fate and short-term biosafety.

item.title: MolValenceX: a browser-based, client-side tool for drawing molecules and estimating aromaticity, CIP stereodescriptors, dipole moments and Hansen solubility parameters, with benchmarking against experimental and reference-toolkit data
item.description: MolValenceX is a free, open-source chemical structure editor and analyser that runs entirely in a web browser, with no installation, server or account. A drawn or imported (SMILES) structure is analysed for molecular formula, molar mass and degree of unsaturation, ring aromaticity by Hückel π-electron counting, R/S configuration with optical-activity assessment from Cahn–Ingold–Prelog (CIP) priorities, E/Z configuration of acyclic double bonds, an empirical bond-moment estimate of the dipole moment from a generated 3D geometry, and Hansen solubility parameters (HSP) with a ranked solvent-compatibility list. All of this is implemented in dependency-free JavaScript. We benchmarked the five predictive modules. Against 23 experimental gas-phase dipole moments (NIST), the dipole module gave a mean absolute error (MAE) of 0.40 D (median 0.17 D; 17 of 23 within 0.5 D), against 0.57 D for a naïve RDKit MMFF/Gasteiger baseline (the difference was not statistically significant, paired Wilcoxon p = 0.057; the bond moments were tuned on small reference molecules, so this is not a strictly held-out comparison). Against 24 handbook HSP sets (23 supported), the mean absolute errors were 0.84 (δD), 2.30 (δP) and 1.61 (δH) MPa½, with a mean Hansen distance Ra of 3.7 MPa½. R/S assignments agreed with the RDKit CIP labeler for 26 of 26 test structures, E/Z for 22 of 24 (the two exceptions are ring double bonds, which the tool does not assess by design), and Hückel ring classification agreed with textbook expectation for 26 of 26 structures. Four large, complex structures are shown as an unvalidated demonstration of scope. The tool is intended for teaching and for quick qualitative screening, not as an analytical reference.

item.title: Implementation of fully automated continuous serial electron diffraction in Instamatic
item.description: Serial electron diffraction, especially when coupled with precession, utilises transmission electron microscopes to reveal crystal structures of beam-sensitive nanocrystals. Unfortunately, its application remains limited due to a lack of a transferable implementation. To address this issue, we added a new data collection protocol to the popular open-source software Instamatic. Utilising a static beam and continuous stage-sliding strategy, the new approach is well suited for high-throughput acquisition across a wide range of supported hardware. The implementation was tested on a model mineral sample, natrolite, producing crystal structure on par with those obtained using established single-crystal methods.

item.title: Capturing many-body effects for metal ions in aqueous phase through developing specialized machine learning force fields
item.description: Metal ion–ligand interactions govern reactivity, bioavailability, and catalytic function across chemistry and biology, yet the many-body effects underlying water exchange around multivalent metal ions remain difficult to capture with classical force fields. Ab initio molecular dynamics (AIMD), by contrast, provides accurate results but is limited to picosecond timescale sampling by its high computational cost. Machine learning force fields (MLFFs) offer a promising route to quantum-mechanics-level accuracy at force-field-level cost, but we show that existing MACE foundation models which were trained on materials predict an incorrect coordination number for Zn2+ in aqueous phase. To address this gap, we developed a CREST-based enhanced-sampling workflow to generate diverse quantum mechanical reference data and trained specialized E(3)-equivariant MACE models for Zn2+, Ca2+, and La3+ in aqueous solution. Systematic benchmarking of DFT functionals, model hyperparameters, data precision, and water geometry shows that model performance is sensitive to several of these choices, underscoring the need for careful validation. Encouragingly, the resulting specialized MACE models accurately reproduce hydration structures, coordination number distributions, and water-exchange kinetics in excellent agreement with experiment and AIMD, outperforming classical force fields (12-6, 12-6-4, and AMOEBA) in simultaneously capturing energetics and mechanism. We further extend this approach to ML/MM simulations of the metalloenzyme thermolysin, reproducing the monodentate/bidentate switching of Glu166 and capturing Zn2+ coordination number flexibility over a 2 ns trajectory—a timescale inaccessible to conventional QM/MM. These results demonstrate that specialized MLFFs provide a practical and transferable strategy for bridging quantum mechanical accuracy with molecular mechanics speed for metal-ligand systems, enabling long-timescale conformational sampling, mutant screening, and mechanistic studies of metalloenzyme catalysis that were previously out of reach.

item.title: MeCoBi: A fast and accurate transition metal complex builder that generates 3D structures at scale and enables structure-based machine learning
item.description: The three-dimensional arrangement of ligands around a metal centre determines its electronic structure, reactivity, and biological activity, yet generating accurate three-dimensional (3D) structures from a ligand list remains difficult. Existing tools tend to be slow, narrow in coverage, or require manual specification. We present MeCoBi (Metal Complex Builder), an automated pipeline that builds and optimises 3D structures of mononuclear metal complexes from ligand SMILES across 36 d-block and main-group metals and coordination numbers 2–9. On 30,830 experimental structures from the Cambridge Structural Database, MeCoBi generated a structure for 99.6% of complexes with a median error in metal–ligand bond lengths of 0.06 Å. We then used the generated structures as inputs for machine learning. For the cytotoxicity of ruthenium complexes from MetalCytoToxDB, a model trained only on the structures came within 0.02 in ROC-AUC of the best model based on two-dimensional descriptors; for the antibacterial activity of a library of 1,800 iridium complexes prepared in our laboratory, it ranked the new complexes better than the 2D descriptor models (ROC-AUC 0.88 against 0.84). For the dipole moments and HOMO–LUMO gaps of 10,175 complexes from the tmQM dataset, adding the results of a GFN2-xTB calculation on the MeCoBi structures to a two-dimensional model lowered its mean absolute error from 1.68 to 1.24 D and 0.367 to 0.311 eV, and the improvement remained for structures built from the SMILES alone. MeCoBi is open source, with a web interface at mecobi.york.ac.uk.

item.title: Adsorption fingerprints of proteins at fluid interfaces: a molecular dynamics study of Lysozyme at water/oil and water/air interfaces
item.description: Protein adsorption at fluid interfaces is central to pharmaceutical formulation, food colloids, and bioprocessing technologies, yet its molecular basis remains poorly understood. We investigate lysozyme (LSZ) adsorption at water-air and water-hexadecane interfaces using molecular dynamics simulations with the all-atom CHARMM36m, united-atom GROMOS53A6, and coarse-grained MARTINI 3 force fields. At the waterair interface, only GROMOS53A6 predicts adsorption of native LSZ within the simulated timescales, whereas CHARMM36m and MARTINI 3 show no stable adsorption within 200 ns and 1 µs, respectively. In contrast, all three models predict adsorption at the water-hexadecane interface, consistent with a stronger thermodynamic driving force for adsorption at oil than at vapor interfaces. item.title: Optical Properties of Monocarboxylic and Dicarboxylic Acids in the Atmosphere
item.description: The optical properties of atmospherically relevant molecular clusters remain elusive, as they are difficult to measure using current experimental techniques. Using quantum chemical methods, we here investigate the absorption and scattering properties of selective organic acid clusters. We studied 185 different (acid)1(Na+)0−2(Cl–)0−1(w)0−5 clusters comprised of the monocarboxylic acids: Pyruvic acid (PA), lactic acid (LA), propionic acid (ProA), and 2,2-dihydroxypropionic acid (diol) and the dicarboxylic acids: Fumaric acid (FA) and maleic acid (MA). We calculated the static and dynamic isotropic and anisotropic polarizabilities and the 10 lowest singlet-state excitation energies at the CAM-B3LYP/aug-cc-pVTZ level of theory. We find that the isotropic and anisotropic polarizabilities effectively depend linearly on the cluster size, with all the data residing within the 95% prediction interval for the linear fits. We also find that the Rayleigh scattering activities depend quadratically on the cluster size, with the quadratic fit being very close to the fit obtained for the inorganic acid–base clusters studied previously. This indicates that the scattering properties of organic and inorganic clusters might be very similar in the atmosphere, solely depending on the polarizability. Finally, we find the clusters to absorb in the ultraviolet (UV) region, with an observed redshift in the spectra of the dicarboxylic acids and negatively charged conjugate bases compared to the monocarboxylic acids, and with only a limited blueshifting effect on the organic acid clusters induced by the presence of Na+ and Cl–ions. However, clusters with stronger chromophore units such as several carbonyl groups, extended π-conjugated systems, and aromatic rings are still necessary in the organic constituents for shifting the cluster absorption towards the visible region of the spectrum.

item.title: Differentiable Search of Compositionally Complex Alloys
item.description: Identifying solid-solution compositions in multicomponent alloys requires exploring a highdimensional design space while accounting for competing phases. We present a differentiable search framework that uses composition gradients of a thermodynamic objective to identify promising alloy regions without exhaustive grid enumeration. In the present implementation, an alchemical machine-learning interatomic potential and ideal configurational entropy provide a differentiable free-energy approximation for random solid solutions. Gradient-based optimization is combined with metadynamics biasing to explore multiple basins, and a tangent-plane criterion screens candidates against precipitation of competing compounds. Applied to the Mg–Al–Sc–Ti–V–Cr–Mn–Fe–Co–Ni system on fcc, bcc, and hcp lattices at 1000 and 1600 K, the search recovers compositionally complex alloy (CCA) families supported by literature. The dominant Cr–Mn–Fe–Co–Ni candidate region expands at 1600 K to include V-containing families and six-principal-element compositions. Screened compositions show substantial departures from equimolarity, highlighting the value of continuous composition optimization. The search also identifies the less-explored Mg–Sc–Ti system, for which preliminary CALPHAD calculations suggest extended high-temperature bcc solid-solution fields under suitable pressure conditions. These results demonstrate a framework for efficient search of CCAs and illustrate how differentiable materials models can serve directly as tools for materials design.

item.title: FLAME: Fluorinated-motif Learning and Attribution for Molecular Explainability Applied to PFAS
item.description: Machine-learning (ML) architectures such as graph neural networks (GNNs) are increasingly used in structure-property modeling and molecular property prediction in fields of emerging contaminants such as per-and polyfluoroalkyl substances (PFAS). However, their black-box nature makes these models difficult to use in scientific interpretation, decision making and in providing identifiable molecular substructures that contributed to the predictions. In attempts to open up the black-box, fragment-based explainability techniques have been created to capture molecular motifs that contributed to the predicted properties. However, these fragment-based explanations are dependent on how the molecular structures are partitioned and general molecular fragmentation methods may not capture highly fluorinated motifs, functional headgroups, and linker environments relevant for PFAS and related fluorinated compounds. The resulting fragment explanations may be less chemically meaningful unless fragmentation approaches account explicitly for the distinctive chemistry of fluorinated molecular motifs. We present Fluorinated-motif Learning and Attribution for Molecular Explainability (FLAME), a PFAS-tailored framework that extends rBRICS fragmentation to improve fragment-based explainability methods. The additional cleavage environments improved the separation of PFASrelevant structures, enabling the separation of 568 additional molecules relative to the original rBRICS in a dataset of 4,738 molecules. The substructure masking explanation method was then applied to a graph neural network that predicted electron affinity, ionization potential, and HOMO–LUMO gap. The chemically tailored fragments provided identifiable units for substructure masking allowing more interpretable predictions based on motif-level attributions. Our results demonstrate a constrained explainability framework built upon chemically relevant structural motifs. FLAME is extensible to other classes of emerging contaminants whose characteristic structural motifs require tailored fragmentation for scientifically meaningful model explanations.

item.title: Electrodes as Tunable Ligands: Electro-Inductive Control of Supported Catalyst Reactivity
item.description: Electronic tuning of molecular catalysts traditionally relies on synthetic modification of ligand structures, with each modification requiring the preparation of a distinct catalyst whose electronic properties are largely fixed at synthesis. Herein, we investigate a complementary strategy in which applied potential serves as a continuously adjustable electronic input to a surface-bound molecular catalyst. A pyridine(diimine) iron catalyst was anchored to TiO2 supported on fluorine-doped tin oxide (FTO) through a conjugated linker that facilitated communication between the active site and the conductive surface. The anchored catalyst was active for the ring-opening polymerization of L-lactide, with polymerization rates increasing under positive applied potential and decreasing under negative applied potential. These results are consistent with an electro-inductive effect in which applied potential modulated the Lewis acidity of the Fe center, supported by trends observed in a complementary Hammett study of para-substituted molecular Fe complexes. Because potential can be varied without altering molecular structure, catalyst activity could also be modified in real time during polymerization. This work demonstrates electro-inductive control of catalytic reactivity for a metal oxide-supported catalyst, illustrating how supported molecular catalysts provide new avenues for dynamically tuning thermochemical catalytic activity.

item.title: Computational Insights into Chiral Induced Spin Selectivity in Organic Semiconductors via Circular Dichroism Prediction
item.description: Due to implications ranging from the origins of chirality in nature to the development of better spintronic devices, there is notable interest in gaining a deeper understanding of the quantum structure property relationships underlying the chiral induced spin-selectivity (CISS) effect. Although many features proposed to contribute heavily to CISS are computationally expensive, studies have shown that the maximum circular dichroism (CD) absorbance correlates strongly with the magnitude of CISS effect exhibited by a material and that time-dependent density functional theory (TD-DFT) methods can accurately predict CD spectra at a reasonable cost. In this work, we present an unprecedented analysis of approximately 1000 organic semiconductive hexamers using a selection of data science and machine learning methods to examine the quantum structure property relationships contributing to high CD response, finding the paramount importance of polarizability and conformational features as determined by selected methods. item.title: On the real role of hydroxide in zeolite crystallization: electrochemically-generated OH synthesis
item.description: Hydrothermal synthesis of zeolites is typically conducted in basic media, where the hydroxide anion (OH-) acts as a mineralizing agent, promoting the transformation of precursors into crystalline frameworks. OH- is introduced together with (in)organic structure-directing agents ((in)OSDAs), thus always accompanied by a counter-cation (e.g., Tetrapropylammonium+, Na+). Consequently, for systems containing only monovalent ions, the OH-/SDA+ ratio generally remains at 1 (or below). Contrary to this common approach, we employed a dual electrochemical cell as a novel, unconventional reactor for the in situ cathodic generation of OH-, termed Electrochemically-generated OH Synthesis (EOS). Demonstrated for the first time, expanding the OH-/OSDA+ ratio from 0.8 to 1.2 at a constant OSDA content during Silicalite-1 crystallization enabled us to decouple the role of OH- from that of the OSDA. Crystal size, solid yield, and OSDA uptake strongly depended on the OH- content, confirming a broader role of OH- than that of a mineralizer. The evolution of silicate precursors, crystallization kinetics, and particularly the nucleation step were witnessed as the most affected parameters. This decoupling further shows that OSDA uptake by pure-silica frameworks is not solely governed by templating, but also depends on the charge state of the precursors, which is directly influenced by OH- content. EOS reveals an alternative gel-mediated precursor pathway prior to Silicalite‑1 crystallization, highlighting the influence of precursor state and crystallization pathway on the final material properties.

item.title: Machine Learning-Guided Comparison of n- and p-Type Reorganization Energies
item.description: A key component in the rational design of novel, high-performing candidate organic electronic materials is understanding and predicting the charge transport properties of π-conjugated materials. Although purely experimental design methods can be prohibitively expensive, previous computational investigations have established cost-saving methods to accurately predict charge transport for π-conjugated materials via internal Marcus reorganization energy. Many works, however, have focused solely on p-type charge transfer, whereas many organic electronic devices utilize both n-and p-type materials or motifs. As such, a deeper understanding of the features that influence n-type charge transport is important. In this work, we present a wholesale machine learning (ML)-driven analysis of n-type charge transport for a previously established dataset of polythiophene derivatives. The performance and results of the model are somewhat similar for the prediction of n-and p-type λs by a random forest regression model, albeit with key differences discussed herein.

item.title: Oxygen-Driven Etching of MAX Phases Assisted by HF Vapor (OxyVap-HF) for MXenes Synthesis
item.description: MXenes are conventionally produced by immersing MAX phases in fluoride-containing acids, where removal of A elements proceeds via their proton-driven oxidation leading to H2 gas evolution accompanied by fluoride complexation with An+. Here we introduce a different, oxygen-driven HF vapor assisted route (OxyVap-HF) in which a precursor MAX phase, such as Ti3AlC2, is held separated from a dilute HF solution reservoir and etched by oxygen available in air, assisted by HF/H2O vapor helping to maintain access of oxygen to A element layers. Importantly, in OxyVap-HF the MAX phase is never in direct contact with liquid, therefore the same dilute HF solution can be used multiple times without purification or any other treatment, minimizing safety risks and environmental burden of MXene synthesis, thereby directly addressing the need for greener MXene synthesis methods. Mechanistically, in the oxygen-containing atmosphere of the OxyVap-HF the etching reaction consumes O2 rather than evolving H2. Gas volume analysis, scavenging of O2 with pyrogallol, experiments in controlled Ar/O2/air atmospheres, and Raman spectroscopy of the gas phase demonstrate a switch from traditional proton-driven, H2-evolving etching under Ar, to oxygen-driven etching in air. The HF/H2O ratio controls MAX phase conversion, assisting with the removal of Al–O-containing intermediates formed during etching, installing terminations, and expanding the interlayer spacing, thus yielding MXenes that can be further delaminated. We show that an aqueous HF solution with concentration as low as 3 wt% can be used repeatedly in OxyVap-HF process, consistently yielding new batches of delaminable MXenes.

item.title: Lorentz-Covariant Bi-Photonic Kinematics: Deriving Optical Polarization and the Born Rule from Internal Constrained Dynamics
item.description: (Dated: November 7, 2026) Standard quantum electrodynamics (QED) treats the photon as an unstructured, point-like excitation of a gauge field. In this orthodox framework, when light encounters a measurement device, its continuous wave description abruptly and unpredictably reduces to a single discrete detector click. The statistical likelihood of recording that click is calculated by squaring the overlap between the incoming wave state and the detector state—an operational prescription universally known as the Born rule (P = |⟨ϕ|ψ⟩|2). The persistent inability of spontaneous collapse hypotheses, context-free hidden-variable schemes, and many-worlds branching to eliminate fundamental unpredictability stems from treating abstract state vectors as irreducible primitives of nature. Here, we formulate a relativistic, composite two-particle (bi-photonic) model of light in which a single optical packet consists of a phase-locked pair of conjugate sub-elements (γA, γB) executing internal transverse orbital motion on a light-cone surface. Using relativistic Hamiltonian mechanics with algebraic constraints (Dirac constraint mechanics), we prove that the negative internal binding potential exactly cancels the positive transverse orbital kinetic energy inside the invariant mass operator.Figure 1Biphotonic kinematic model of one quantum of light.Biphotonic model of a single light packet. item.title: Integrated Computational Design and Multistage Virtual Screening for the Prioritization of Putative USP5 Catalytic-Cleft Inhibitors
item.description: Ubiquitin-specific protease 5 (USP5) processes unanchored polyubiquitin and has been linked to cancer-associated signaling. We developed a computer-aided workflow to generate and rank small molecules against its catalytic/substrate cleft. The starting dataset contained 26 activity records representing 19 unique compounds, ten with measured half-maximal inhibitory concentrations. Descriptor-based quantitative structure-activity relationship models underwent compound leave-one-out and scaffold-held-out validation. Ten chemical-enumeration methods produced 3,646 method–product records and 3,264 unique structures. The main screen combined these structures with ten additional source-positive molecules and retained 18 compounds under strict selection criteria. A ten-compound panel, comprising nine generated structures and one known benchmark, underwent corrected AutoDock Vina docking against two USP5 receptor copies. The primary and repeated-seed campaigns produced 800 recorded modes. Standard-precision (SP) and extra-precision (XP) Glide docking independently evaluated the prepared ligand library, followed by Prime molecular mechanics/generalized Born surface area (MM-GBSA) calculations on the XP complexes. P06 emerged as the top-ranked candidate in the three-stage consensus analysis, ranking first in SP and second in both XP and MM-GBSA evaluations. P03 achieved the most favorable mean XP docking score, whereas P09 exhibited the strongest mean MM-GBSA binding energy. P10 ranked third overall but demonstrated greater sensitivity to receptor conformation. Collectively, this integrated computational workflow establishes a prioritized hierarchy of candidate compounds targeting the USP5 catalytic/substrate-binding cleft and highlights the influence of chemical selection and receptor preparation on structure-based rankings.

item.title: Dataset-level reliability and quality control for metallurgical data structured with large language models
item.description: Data-driven alloy design depends on the availability of reliable, structured experimental information. Although the scientific literature contains large volumes of such data, heterogeneous reporting practices hinder their systematic reuse at scale. General-purpose large language models (LLMs) offer a flexible approach for structuring metallurgical text without domain-specific fine-tuning, but they introduce errors such as omissions, misassignments, and fabrications that are not fully characterised by conventional extraction metrics. This study examines error behaviour in LLM-assisted extraction of metallurgical information using a multi-stage workflow comprising text classification, structured extraction, and automated review. Controlled experiments are used to analyse how prompt design, task formulation, and reporting structure influence error behaviour within each stage of the workflow. The workflow is subsequently evaluated at large scale on a corpus of 23,861 full-text publications on high-chromium steels, combining automated reviewer signals with statistically grounded manual sampling to assess residual errors. The results identify dominant, task-dependent error modes and show that similar extraction performance can correspond to substantially different uncertainty profiles across information types. These findings clarify how error behaviour depends on text structure and task formulation and provide a basis for the risk-aware reuse of literature-derived metallurgical data.

item.title: Expanding the Covalent Warhead Toolbox: Discovery of the First Covalent PARG Inhibitors Using Bicyclo[1.1.0]butane-Based Warheads
item.description: Poly(ADP-ribose) glycohydrolase (PARG) is the principal enzyme responsible for the degradation of poly(ADP-ribose) chains and has emerged as a promising therapeutic target in oncology within the DNA damage response (DDR) field. Although several reversible PARG inhibitors have recently entered clinical development, covalent inhibition of PARG has not previously been described. Herein, we report the discovery and optimization of the first covalent PARG inhibitors. Guided by structural analysis of the PARG catalytic domain, electrophilic warheads were incorporated into reversible quinazolinedione-based inhibitors to enable selective engagement of Cys872, a residue located within the catalytic pocket. While unsaturated ketone and hydrazide warheads enabled covalent inhibition of PARG, incorporation of a bicyclo[1.1.0]butane (BCB) hydrazide warhead led to the discovery of FORX-175, combining potent biochemical and cellular activity, reduced electrophile reactivity, and improved covalent-labeling selectivity. To the best of our knowledge, this work represents the first application of a BCB hydrazide warhead for selective covalent cysteine targeting. Building on these findings, a hybrid design strategy combining structural elements of the covalent quinazolinedione series with those of a reversible PARG inhibitor series led to the discovery of FORX-425, a covalent quinoline inhibitor bearing an underexplored BCB-carboxamide warhead. FORX-425 displayed potent biochemical inhibition, efficient covalent engagement, and nanomolar cellular activity in PARG-sensitive cancer cell lines. Collectively, these studies establish covalent inhibition as a viable strategy for PARG modulation, identify Cys872 as a tractable site for selective covalent targeting, and further demonstrate the potential of BCB-derived warheads for cysteine-directed drug discovery.

item.title: Controlled Oxidant Delivery Uncovers Selectivity Branching in Heterogeneous Epoxidation Catalysis
item.description: Heterogeneous catalysis generally features complex speciation of reactive intermediates that limits selectivity control and mechanistic understanding. Olefin epoxidation is a major and highly carbon-intensive process in the chemical industry, yet the molecular origin of selectivity branching causing the competing, CO2-emitting combustion reaction remains debated and is obscured by the presence of multiple oxidants on catalyst surfaces. Herein, we selectively generated surface metaloxygen (M–O) species, a commonly proposed intermediate, and discovered clean, O2-dependent chemoselectivity: surface M–O alone exhibited up to 100% selectivity toward epoxidation, whereas the co-existence of surface M–O and O2 could lead to combustion via a novel oxidative C=C cleavage pathway. Further studies uncovered unprecedented insights into selectivity branching, suggesting new strategies for rationally decarbonizing epoxidation catalysis.

item.title: 3-Methyl-2-Oxazolidinone (MOX), an Effective and Plausibly Green Solvent Replacement for DMF in Amidation Reactions
item.description: The solvent N,N-dimethylformamide (DMF) is widely used in organic synthesis for a broad range of chemical reactions. However, prolonged exposure to DMF presents serious health hazards due to its hepatotoxicity and reproductive toxicity. Growing appreciation of these risks has motivated public and private institutions to phase out the use of DMF and identify safe, viable alternatives for various applications. This is especially urgent for amidation, the most frequently performed reaction class in pharmaceutical organic synthesis, for which DMF is the most frequently used solvent. Existing alternatives to DMF have distinct chemical or practical drawbacks, discouraging widespread adoption. Herein, we identify 3-methyl-2-oxazolidinone (MOX), an unexplored polar aprotic solvent with a favorable chemical, safety, and sustainability profile, as a general replacement for DMF in the synthesis of amides from amines and carboxylic acids. MOX was evaluated in solution-phase amidation reactions for the synthesis of dipeptides, active pharmaceutical ingredients, synthetic auxiliaries, and other structurally or electronically diverse substrates. Across 44 examples employing 23 coupling agents or coupling methods, MOX enabled amidation reactions for a chemically diverse set of substrates through a broad range of reaction conditions. Isolated yields ranged from 43–98%, with a mean yield of 81%. Optimization of reaction conditions was rarely required. These findings establish MOX as a safe and practical replacement for DMF in amidation reactions. Introduction

item.title: Stereoelectronic Modulation of Hyperconjugative Networks in Saturated Heterocycles: Bridging Hilbert-Space NBO Perturbations with Real-Space QTAIM Electron Cloud Distortions
item.description: The stereoelectronic modulation of hyperconjugative networks dictates the fundamental parameters of saturated heterocycles. Herein is presented a quantum chemical investigation into the anomeric effect across a matrix of 2-substituted oxygen and sulfur heterocycles utilising a GPU-accelerated pySCF-GPU optimisation pipeline at the CAM-B3LYP-D3(BJ)/def2-TZVPD/PCM level of theory, coupled with orbital perturbation evaluations via Firefly B3LYP-D3(BJ)/def2-TZVPD; QTAIM topology analyses via Multiwfn. For the axial 2-fluoro anomer, the exo-anomeric effect is heavily magnified; NBO maps a massive (no → σ*C-F) stabilisation energy (E(2) = 20.11 kcal/mol). Real-space QTAIM maps confirm the physical consequences of this; compared to a standard C-C baseline (∇²ρbcp ~= -0.6328 a.u.), the active C3-O2 bond exhibits a π-like charge concentration spike (∇²ρbcp = -0.8182 a.u., LBO = 0.503, e = 0.1396), while the adjacent C-F bond is thinned and flattened (∇²ρbcp = -0.3401 a.u., LBO = 0.107, e = 0.1827). Conversely, oxo-protonation triggers the anti-anomeric effect. Sequestering the dominant lone pair into a stable σO-H bond quenches the exo engine, leaving a residual contribution from the σ-type lone pair and driving an intensive internal (nF → σ*C-O) back-donation (E(2) = 17.38 kcal/mol), that forces the endocyclic bond relaxation to 1.483 Å in the anti-oxonium conformer.

item.title: Hard X-ray Studio for reproducible analysis of static and modulated excitation X-ray absorption spectroscopy
item.description: Quick-scanning X-ray Absorption Spectroscopy (QXAFS) is an emerging technique recent year, which enables complete XAS to be acquired on sub-second to second timescales, providing a powerful means of probing transient electronic and local structural changes under operando conditions. We present Hard X-ray Studio, a local application combining a browser interface with a Python and XrayLarch service. Static mode prepares individual spectra or merges reviewed repeats into named conditions before feature extraction. Time-series mode retains acquisition coordinates and supports electrochemical synchronization, phase-sensitive detection and kinetic analysis. Both modes provide calibrated preparation, constrained XANES linear-combination fitting (LCF), singular-value decomposition (SVD) and multivariate curve resolution (MCR), and EXAFS extraction with relative shell descriptors. A kinetic-analysis module applies exponential models to both the excitation response and time-dependent spectral descriptors, allowing their characteristic time constants to be compared and their consistency to be evaluated. The platform links these analyses through stable source identities, explicit selections and processing-state checks. Its distinctive design preserves missing metadata and source membership while distinguishing condition comparisons from temporal responses. These reproduce imposed mixture fractions, periodic amplitudes, relative EXAFS descriptors and response rates. Experimental NiFe-LDH measurements analysed in Origin provide a separate reference case for subsequent numerical comparison. Hard X-ray Studio offers an inspectable workflow for connecting static and time-resolved XAS analyses while retaining measurements locally; experimental benchmarking and deployment acceptance remain distinct from numerical verification.

item.title: Optimal control of lipid–peroxyl radical-pair termination under spin relaxation
item.description: Spin-selective radical-pair reactions provide a molecular mechanism through which magnetic fields can influence chemical kinetics, but whether a shaped field can retain a control advantage under spin relaxation and molecular motion remains open. We address this question for the termination of lipid autoxidation chains through spin-selective encounters between lipid-peroxyl radicals, connecting optimal control of the radical pair to explicit Brownian dynamics and to classical autoxidation kinetics. Gradient-projection optimization, corroborated by a bang–bang Pontryagin solution, identifies a dipolar-scale operating range: the best-found field raises the triplet-initialized singlet termination yield from ΦS|T = 0.220 at 50 µT to 0.562 (+155%), with the bang–bang solution reaching 0.522 and a bandwidth-filtered proxy retaining 0.270. An idealized stochastic-Schrödinger relaxation model serves as a stress test, whereas explicit Brownian dynamics treats the molecular motion; under Brownian dynamics the control advantage remains positive throughout the sampled rotational-correlation-time range, and one field transfers across eight microdomain-size–diffusion parameter sets. Closing the spin calculation to classical autoxidation kinetics gives Ceff = −f/(1+f), where f is the fraction of peroxyl loss proceeding through bimolecular termination. Two limiting descriptions of the productive-encounter spin composition bracket the predicted suppression of oxidation flux in antioxidant-free liposomes at approximately 21–37%, and at approximately 4–10% for the bandwidth-filtered field. α-Tocopherol attenuates the response as interception comes to dominate, providing an internal experimental control. These values describe an elementary encounter and a minimal kinetic model, not whole-cell lipid peroxidation.

item.title: Core-to-rim chemical zoning of a Paraíbatype tourmaline from Abulo, Ethiopia: Implications for origin determination
item.description: Copper-bearing tourmaline of Paraíba type is now mined at Abulo in southern Ethiopia. We report the core-to-rim characterisation of one colour-zoned crystal attributed to this locality, obtained in Bangkok in June 2026. A sawn slab about 12 mm across and 5 mm thick was extensively analysed by electron microprobe (113 points), LA-ICP-MS analysis (45 spots on two traverses and 58 isotopes, totaling 2,565 concentration values with silicon as internal standard and GSE and NIST 610 as external standards), LA-ICP-TOFMS imaging (13,500 measuring spots of 24 µm and 55 isotopes, totalling 729,000 concentration values with silicon as internal standard and GSE and NIST 610 as external standard, about 505,000 of them above limits of detection), Raman spectroscopy (24 spectra) and a screening test by ED-XRF. The crystal is an Al–Li tourmaline of the elbaite series, including elbaite, fluor-elbaite, and elbaite with a liddicoatite component. Fluorine at the W site is 0.385 apfu in the core and exceeds the 0.5 apfu boundary to fluor-elbaite in the zones next to the core (0.51–0.53 apfu); 25 of 111 points lie within 1σ of that boundary. Ca/(Ca + Na) increases from core to rim but never exceeds 0.43. Lithium, measured by LA-ICP-MS, increases from about 7,840 µg/g in the core to about 10,000 µg/g in the outer zones. With this lithium taken zone by zone, boron and H2O taken from the formula and the unanalysed trace elements added as oxides, the analytical totals of the microprobe are 99.2 ± 0.5 wt.% over 111 points. The trace elements are quantified on this measured matrix, with silicon measured by microprobe as internal standard using GSE and NIST610 as external standards. To our knowledge for the first time, silicon concentrations were measured across a growth profile of this material, in each of the five growth zones of the crystal. The measurements provide 36.3 wt.% SiO2 in the core, 35.2–35.4 wt.% in the dark-blue zone, 35.5–35.8 wt% in the "neon"-blue zone, 35.9 wt% in the pink zone and 36.0 wt% in the yellow-brown zone. The concentrations of the trace elements are significantly zoned. Copper zone averages decrease from 16,200–25,700 µg/g in the core and the dark-blue zones around it to 1,420–1,820 µg/g in the yellow-brown outer zone. The iron concentration decreases from 4,130–4,150 µg/g to below detection. The bismuth concentration increases from 26–27 to 1,370 µg/g and the lead concentration from 146–160 to 1,650–1,810 µg/g. In contrast , gallium (629–741 µg/g as zone averages) and vanadium (58–158 µg/g at all 45 spots) vary far less. The element ratios used in origin determination therefore change by up to an order of magnitude inside this one crystal. For example, Cu/Ga changes from 2.3 to 41, Pb/Bi from 1.2 to 5.9 and Fe/Mn starts below detection to 1.1 which are calculated as zone averages. The imaging confirms the element ratios of the spot analyses and separates the elements that are present in the tourmaline's composition from those carried by inclusions, which are detected above the matrix composition of the tourmaline. Of the rare earth elements, only the light rare earths, La to Sm, are present in the tourmaline's composition. Yttrium is also present in the tourmaline, at about 0.6–0.9 µg/g outside the core and lower in the core. The other elements found in the tourmaline include Li, Be, Sn, Ga, Nb, Ta and B, all of which are typically found in LCT pegmatites. Compared with our 2009 reference profiles for Brazil, Mozambique and Nigeria, the crystal from Ethopia has higher vanadium and gallium concentrations and evolves toward bismuth rather than manganese. A high vanadium concentration is independently reported for Ethiopian material by other laboratories, and the vanadium test proposed there holds across the growth zones of this crystal, with the core at the limitofdetection. The gallium difference from Mozambique is small, whereas the published Ethiopian gallium concentration extends to 280 µg/g. Because the comparison is based on a very detailed analysis of five growth zones, the reported observations are very significant and represent more information than the analyses of larger sample sets. Therefore, this information is crucial as origin criteria. Individual analyses of samples could represent mixtures of various growth zones and would not easily be identified without knowledge about the growth stage. Any discriminant therefore has to be implemented into the growth-stage concentration profiles of this study as reference. A limited Raman data set, placed on the element maps, shows that the framework bands shift with the copper concentration and that the OH bands follow the fluorine and lithium concentrations; these relations are shown for one crystal.

item.title: Backbone Expansion via Enzyme-Mediated Side-Chain Transfer
item.description: There exists no straightforward strategy to generate protein materials containing internally spliced non-protein matter, especially at lengths and scales that support functional characterization. Here we describe Backbone Expansion via Enzyme-mediated Side-chain Transfer (BEST), a facile and general strategy for generating proteins containing internally spliced, non-protein matter at scale. Protein substrates for BEST contain a reactive glutamine (Gln), a backbone ester linkage, and a non-canonical side chain carrying a bioorthogonal reaction handle; the latter two elements are easily installed using a non-canonical ⍺-hydroxy acid. The bioorthogonal side chain is first extended via a click reaction with an element of non-protein matter that terminates in a primary amine. Treatment of this side-chain extended protein with transglutaminase (TGase) results in an intramolecular reaction between the glutamine side chain and the primary amine, generating an ester-containing macrocycle; selective cleavage of the macrocycle under basic conditions inserts the non-protein matter into the backbone with a minimal scar. Thus rather than excising an internal sequence element to restore polypeptide backbone continuity as in an intein-catalyzed reaction, BEST inserts diverse non-protein matter between two neighboring residues and subsequently cleaves the backbone between them. By transforming the protein backbone itself into an addressable locus for synthetic macromolecular integration, BEST establishes a general framework for constructing protein-polymer hybrids in which abiotic matter is not appended to a protein but structurally encoded within.

item.title: From Cell to Pack: Experimental Validation of a Thermo-Electrochemical 4s4p Battery Model
item.description: Growing deployment of lithium-ion batteries has intensified the need for advanced battery pack simulation tools to address the key engineering challenge of accurately predicting the electrical and thermal behaviour of battery packs. This work presents a scalable, physics-based simulation framework for arbitrary (Ms, Np) lithium-ion battery pack configurations. The framework is demonstrated and experimentally validated using a 4s4p pack with bottom cooling. Experiments were conducted on the pack, with temperatures measured throughout the assembly using 80 thermal sensors distributed uniformly across the pack. The resulting spatially and temporally resolved temperature measurements, together with measured pack voltage, are compared directly with model predictions obtained using both the standard expression for irreversible heat generation and the energetically consistent expression derived in [27], which includes heat of mixing within the electrode particles. The heat-transfer model is parametrised using a charge–discharge protocol that yields the same heat-transfer coefficients for both heating formulations. The standard expression gives only moderate agreement with the measured temperatures, whereas simulations using the energetically consistent expression show very good agreement with both the temperature evolution across the pack and its electrical response. The approach represents each cell as a set of spatially resolved finite sections, each governed by the full Doyle–Fuller–Newman (DFN) equations, with all sections coupled thermally and electrically. For the 4s4p case, this results in a network of 80 simultaneously solved DFN models. This formulation enables detailed prediction of intra-pack thermal and electrochemical behaviour. The simulation platform is implemented as a flexible API. The resulting tool can support the design of more reliable and longer-lasting lithium-ion battery systems across a range of large-scale applications.

item.title: Decoupled Semisolid Extrusion and Drop-on-Demand Dispensing for Liposomal Nanomedicine Tableting
item.description: Distributed manufacturing of personalized oral nanomedicines requires processing that protects delicate nanocarriers from thermal and mechanical degradation. Tableting of liposomal nanomedicine into solid dosage forms has gained interest by providing enhanced physicochemical stability and room temperature storage, simplifying cold-chain logistics. Nanomedicine advancements have corresponded with the recent push toward an agile decentralized manufacturing paradigm, incorporating additive manufacturing and 3D printing technologies. This study presents a quality by design-guided framework that decouples semisolid extrusion of blank tablet vehicles from drop-on-demand (DoD) microdispensing of liquid liposomal inks. Critical material attributes and critical process parameters were systematically investigated and optimized to preserve liposomal integrity using a lipid bilayer permeability disruption assay and dynamic light scattering size measurements. Decoupling tablet fabrication from the pharmaceutical drug dosing limited the maximum internal processing temperatures to approximately 50 °C for under 5 minutes, safeguarding the thermolabile liposomes. DoD microdispensing across varying nozzle diameters (60 µm and 100 µm) and pressure pulse intensities (5 Pa·s to 30 Pa·s) produced negligible hydrodynamic shear disruption, maintaining bilayer integrity and liposome particle size distribution. Incorporation into solid tablet matrices enhanced 30-day liposome stability at room temperature relative to aqueous controls, which 2 exhibited membrane breakdown after 14 days. Final tableted formulations, including liposomal ciprofloxacin, met United States Pharmacopeia standards for content uniformity, yielding acceptance values ≤ 8.0 % and target dose recoveries within 90 % to 110 %. This decoupled additive manufacturing platform establishes a robust strategy for decentralized, on-demand compounding of shear- and temperature-sensitive solid oral nanomedicines.

item.title: From Local Motifs to Long-Range Order: Adaptive Diffusion of the Complex Au–S Surface Reconstruction
item.description: Surface reconstructions present a challenging structure-prediction problem because locally favorable atomic motifs must be accommodated within the periodicity of the underlying crystal, often producing large and complex surface unit cells. Here, we extend adaptive diffusion to jointly explore continuous atomic coordinates and discrete surface cell transformations, allowing favorable atomic arrangements and periodicities to be discovered together. We demonstrate the approach for the complex sulfur-induced reconstruction of Au(111), whose atomic structure has remained debated despite extensive experimental investigation. The search identifies a particularly stable rectangular Au4S4 motif and a preference for a transformed surface cell. The exploration also reveals how favorable motifs can be transferred between different periodic environments. Guided by this observation, we construct and relax an arrangement of ten Au4S4 motifs in the experimentally observed large quasi-rectangular unit cell that reproduces the reported sulfur coverage, and is consistent with the local ordering observed by scanning tunneling microscopy.

item.title: Comparative O-Glycosylation Analysis of Etanercept Originator and Biosimilars Using Orthogonal LC-MS Workflows
item.description: Etanercept is a highly glycosylated Fc-fusion protein whose dense, heterogeneous O-glycosylation is challenging to characterize yet relevant to biosimilarity assessment. We compared O-glycosylation in five originator (Enbrel) batches, three biosimilars (Erelzi, Benepali and Nepexto) and the EDQM chemical reference standard using orthogonal LCMS workflows on an Orbitrap Excedion Pro BioPharma mass spectrometer. Native intact mass analysis after N-glycan and sialic acid removal, and middle-up analysis after IdeS digestion, characterized O-glycan macroheterogeneity together with C-terminal lysine and N-terminal leucine-loss variants. Site-specific mapping combined the O-glycoproteases OgpA and IMPa with HCD-triggered EThcD fragmentation. The same 13 O-glycosites were identified in every sample, carrying predominantly sialylated core 1 O-glycans (72%-80% sialylated) with low levels of Tn antigen. In contrast, Benepali and Nepexto showed lower O-glycan occupancy (approximately 17.3 versus 18.9-19.1 O-glycans per molecule) and broader glycoform distributions, and Benepali showed markedly elevated leucine loss (35% of TNF domains). Subunit analysis resolved nearisobaric leucine-loss and di-lysine variants that were ambiguous at the intact level, while EThcD localized O-glycans within densely glycosylated peptides. This multi-level workflow provides a generalizable approach for site-specific O-glycosylation analysis and comparability assessment of O-glycosylated biotherapeutics.

item.title: Polarization Is Required to Model Electrostatic Preorganization: The Case of Chorismate Mutase
item.description: Electrostatic preorganization contributes to enzymatic catalysis through transition state stabilization and is often investigated using classical molecular dynamics (MD) simulations that employ fixed-charge force fields (FFs). Although polarizable FFs allow for more accurate quantification of local electrostatic effects, whether they qualitatively differ from fixed-charge FFs regarding properties such as the substrate conformation stabilized by the enzyme's electrostatics remains unclear. Here, we compare molecular dynamics simulations of chorismate mutase performed with the AMOEBA polarizable FF and the AMBER fixed-charge FF. We find that simulations using AMOEBA sample chorismate geometries resembling the transition state-like near attack conformation (NAC), while AMBER simulations sample strictly non-NAC conformations. The local substrate-protein interactions are also completely altered by the choice of FF, with AMOEBA and AMBER each sampling distinct active site hydrogen bond networks. Finally, even at matched reactive substrate conformations, the heterogeneous three-dimensional electric field experienced by the substrate is qualitatively different between the FFs. By additionally comparing to a modified AMOEBA FF with the induced dipole term turned off, we also isolate the explicit polarization in AMOEBA as the key contributor to these differences.

item.title: Large Language Models in Chemistry: Opportunities, Limitations, and Hallucination Risks
item.description: Large language models (LLMs) have moved quickly from general-purpose text tools to components of chemical research workflows. They are now used to extract data from the literature, propose synthesis routes, write analysis code, predict properties from few examples, and control laboratory instruments through tool-augmented agents. These capabilities create real opportunities, particularly for researchers and institutions with limited access to specialist software and training. They also carry risks that are specific to chemistry. Chemical information is dense with symbols, units, stoichiometry, and safety-critical numbers, and LLMs generate fluent text whether or not it is correct. This perspective reviews the main opportunities for LLMs in chemistry, the technical limitations that constrain them, and a taxonomy of hallucination types with examples of how each can cause harm in a laboratory or research setting. It then proposes a practical verification framework for everyday users, a set of reporting practices for authors, and a short research agenda. The central argument is that LLMs are most valuable in chemistry when they are treated as fallible assistants wrapped in verification tools, such as cheminformatics libraries, databases, and physical measurement, and not as sources of chemical truth.

item.title: Sequence order controls silver(I) coordination in aqueous His–Met–Pro tripeptide–nitrate mixtures: an ab initio molecular dynamics study
item.description: Silver–peptide interactions underpin peptide-directed synthesis of silver nanomaterials and the silver-resistance machinery of bacteria, yet the molecular-level speciation of Ag(I) in the presence of short peptides and nitrate remains poorly resolved. Here we report 100-ps ab initio molecular dynamics simulations of three sequence isomers of the tripeptide His–Met–Pro (HMP, HPM and PHM; 220 atoms each) in water, with four Ag(I) ions, four nitrate anions and 32 water molecules at 298 K, using the PBE–PAW description (VASP 6.1.0, 500 eV plane-wave cutoff, Γ-point sampling). In all three systems silver remains mononuclear, with average coordination numbers of 2.6–2.9 and only transient Ag–Ag contacts (present in 2–9% of frames at a 3.2 Å cutoff). The composition of the coordination shell is strongly sequence-dependent: His–Met–Pro is dominated by the His imidazole nitrogen (0.48 contacts per Ag) and nitrate oxygen (0.57), whereas His–Pro–Met is dominated by the Met thioether sulfur (0.73) with nitrate largely excluded (0.16); Pro–His–Met shows an intermediate, mixed N/S/nitrate shell and the largest peptide conformational rearrangement (heavy-atom RMSD 6.1 Å, radius of gyration 5.8 Å). Nitrate and water exchange on ∼0.2–1 ps timescales, while peptide N/S donors remain bound for several to tens of picoseconds. These results demonstrate that, at fixed composition, sequence order controls which donors are presented to Ag(I) and therefore the speciation from which silver nanomaterials nucleate.

item.title: Monomer sequence influences electron transport in aromatic amide foldamers
item.description: Sequence encodes structure and function in biomolecules, but whether monomer order influences electron transport in synthetic foldamers remains incompletely understood. Here, we investigate aromatic amide foldamers built from a peptide-inspired secondary amide and its N-methylated peptoid-inspired analogue. Single molecule conductance measurements reveal that the all-secondary-amide foldamer exhibits a well-defined conductance state (~10-3.8 G0), comparable to the substantially shorter secondary-amide building block (~10-3.7 G0), whereas incorporation of N-methylated units produces lower or less-defined conductance features. Notably, foldamers with identical composition but different sequence arrangements exhibit distinct conductance distributions, demonstrating that sequence order influences electron transport. Displacement and flicker noise analyses indicate compact junction geometries with substantial throughspace contributions, and the all secondary amide foldamer responds most strongly to changes in applied bias and molecular concentration. Computational modeling using molecular dynamics (MD) simulations, density functional theory (DFT), and nonequilibrium Green's function (NEGF)-DFT calculations provide insight into sequencedependent conformational variability. Overall, this work demonstrates that oligomerization can generate electron transport behavior that cannot be inferred directly from isolated monomer properties and establishes monomer order as a design variable for molecular electronics.

item.title: Probabilistic Design and Safety-Constrained Optimization of a Firewater-Powered Portable Valve Actuation System
item.description: Almost every hazardous facility owns a pressurized, regularly inspected source of hydraulic power: its firewater system. This study asks whether a portable water-hydraulic operator driven through a fire hose can stroke seized or stiff valves without overloading the stem or taking the water that firefighting needs, and which design and operating rules make that likely. A Monte Carlo model with an explicit hydraulic circuit, motor leakage, a relief valve and the surge on stall is evaluated on 200,000 draws; every added mechanism can be switched off, recovering the earlier first-order model exactly. Under assumed input distributions a baseline tool (200 cc, 250:1, 60 gpm) completes the stroke in 75% of the draws but without exceeding the allowable stem torque in only 63%, because a median surge of 45 psi accompanies the stall; a stroke needs about 1,600 L of water. A hose-side accumulator and a relief chart set from the stem strength reduce the over-torque probability to 1% (motor speed at most 3,000 rpm) at a cost of 3 to 9 percentage points of safe strokes, of which a slow creep flow at the start and end of travel recovers 4 to 6. The surge model reproduces classical water-hammer results. The optimum holds out of sample but not under a stem 30% weaker than its data sheet (14% over-torque), and the 2 firefighting reserve is protected only if the spare flow of the source is known. The results are simulation outputs under assumed priors, not measurements.

item.title: Measuring chemical safety and refusal in language models
item.description: A language model can decline a chemistry question for several reasons. It may detect a safety concern, fail to identify the molecule, or lack the facts needed to answer. When it does answer, the response may still be wrong or incomplete. Chemical safety evaluations need to distinguish these outcomes before interpreting differences between models. We propose a framework for doing so, using established practices from cheminformatics: verified identities and reference answers, suitable controls and baselines, independent validation, and statistics that account for related molecules and repeated measurements. We examine chemical safety studies, including SynthRefusal within onepot-Bench 0, ChemSafetyBench, DualChem, and broader scientific safety benchmarks. Eight detailed audits and additional methods readings identify both effective controls and gaps in the evidence. Our reanalyses reproduce large effects of molecular identifiers in ChemIDBench and system prompts in XSTest. A calculation from DualChem shows how excluding tool failures changes the apparent benefit of web access. Because these studies measure different outcomes, we do not pool their results. We propose an experiment that holds legitimate chemical safety questions fixed while changing the identifier and the information supplied to the model. It measures refusal and answer quality together, with separate judgments of whether withholding is appropriate. Separate extensions would test unsafe compliance and, where relevant, practical execution. Each proposed control addresses a specific uncertainty in interpreting model behavior.

item.title: Beyond Ion Features: Resolving Ion Redundancy for LC–HRMS/MS
item.description: Untargeted LC–HRMS/MS workflows frequently represent the same molecular entity through multiple ion features, including adducts, multimers, dehydrated species, and signals compatible with in-source fragmentation. This ion redundancy can propagate into downstream analyses, increasing apparent molecular-network complexity and contributing to unannotated features. To address this issue, we developed two workflows integrated into Compound Discoverer. The unresolved workflow enables structured export of MS2 spectra in MGF format with matched quantitative data, metadata, and an audit trail, whereas the resolved workflow performs ionredundancy resolution and representative-feature selection before export. The approach was evaluated using two reference-standard panels, comprising phytocannabinoids and novel psychoactive substances (NPS), and applied to plant, biological, and in vitro drug-metabolism datasets. Ion-redundancy patterns varied across chemical classes and analytical contexts, encompassing alternative ion species, predefined mass-difference relationships, and MS2-child matches, identified when the m/z of a lower-mass coeluting feature matched a product ion in the MS2 spectrum of a higher-mass feature. Across applications, the resolved workflow reduced exported MGF entries by 18.2–36.1%. In molecular networking, the workflow reshaped molecular-family composition and connectivity through spectral-quality filtering, feature removal, and representative-ion reassignment, while preserving chromatographically distinct features lacking sufficient evidence of redundancy. These findings suggest that LC–HRMS/MS feature space does not necessarily reflect the underlying molecular space. By addressing ion redundancy before spectral export, these workflows provide a conservative and traceable framework that reduces analytical complexity, addresses a potential contributor to the apparent dark metabolome, and enables a more interpretable spectral representation that may better reflect underlying molecular diversity.

item.title: Extended Inter-laboratory Characterization of the New Coastal Seawater Dissolved Organic Matter Reference Material TRM-0522
item.description: Dissolved organic matter (DOM) reference materials are critical to ensuring reliable comparability of measurements across experiments and between labs. TRM-0522, isolated in 2022 from 45 m deep seawater off of Sweden’s west coast, fills the niche of a previously unavailable coastal marine DOM reference material. After its isolation, we detailed a limited number of metrics for TRM-0522, initially disclosing Orbitrap high-resolution mass spectrometry, nuclear magnetic resonance, carbon proportion, absorbance, and fluorescence data. With TRM-0522 becoming more widely used, a variety of labs have generated different metrics that help to characterize and define the chemical properties of this coastal reference material. Here, we disclose TRM-0522 data from elemental analysis, isotopic analysis (δ13C and Δ14C signatures), condensed aromatic “black” carbon characterization, ultra-HRMS (10-21 Tesla FT-ICR-MS and Orbitrap Fusion Lumos), CD3 labelling, and contribution of carbonyls in absorbance and fluorescence after NaBH4 reduction, pH titration, and nitroxide quenching. This greatly expanded dataset reinforces TRM-0522’s suitability as a coastal reference material, and provides metrics for future use between labs and for inevitable additional large-scale collections of material from this site.

item.title: Spatiotemporal Decoupling of Antimicrobial and Osteogenic Cues for Tissue Regeneration: Evidence, Design Windows, and a Validation Roadmap
item.description: Infected bone defects require two outcomes that can conflict at the same site: reduction of biofilm-associated bacterial burden, which usually needs high local antimicrobial exposure, and regeneration of vascularised bone, which needs viable progenitor cells and a resolving immune environment. Biomaterials that present antimicrobial and regenerative cues together are clinically established, but in some systems the exposure needed to act on biofilm may approach the tolerance of host cells. This targeted narrative review develops spatiotemporal decoupling, the separation of cues in time, location or activation condition, as a design hypothesis rather than a proven superior strategy. It (i) defines decoupling operationally and classifies published platforms accordingly; (ii) frames the therapeutic window as a measurable exposure problem, defines exposure metrics, and specifies what must be measured to compute them; (iii) maps four overlapping biological domains (bacterial burden, inflammation, vascular supply, bone formation) to cues, controls and readouts, with each design rule tagged by evidence status; (iv) examines the immuneosteogenic–vascular network as a hypothesis map; (v) positions bioactive glasses and glass-ceramics as a testable platform opportunity, separating what has been shown from what is inferred; and (vi) sets out validation gates and author-proposed reporting recommendations. Most evidence reviewed is mechanistic or preclinical, and matched comparisons against equal-payload co-delivery remain the decisive missing experiment.

item.title: Chemistry-Informed Transfer and Interaction-Resolved Learning Towards Data-Efficient Materials Exploration
item.description: Optimizing synthesis parameters for new thin-film materials is slow and often relies on intuition and trial and error. Gaussian process (GP) models suit low-data settings, but treat each material separately or need engineered descriptors to learn across materials. Multi-task GPs share information across materials but infer these relationships solely from sparse data, making them unreliable early on. We introduce a chemistry-informed multi-task GP that derives these relationships from a Tanimoto kernel on molecular fingerprints, enabling knowledge transfer without descriptor engineering. In closed-loop, uncertaintydriven exploration of a seven-dimensional synthesis space, comprising one categorical variable (three chiral 2D hybrid organic-inorganic perovskite compositions) and six continuous synthesis parameters, we tested 287 conditions (<0.1% of the discretized synthesis space). Knowledge transfer matched the accuracy of single-task GPs trained on the full target dataset using between 35-60% of the target data. Interaction analysis revealed a three-way coupling among annealing temperature, precursor concentration, and composition. This coupling makes a one-variable-at-a-time optimization challenging. Our framework offers a simple strategy for transferring and interpreting knowledge across related materials.

item.title: Advanced High-Throughput Characterization of Nanoporous Materials using Pore Graphs
item.description: Nanoporous materials databases now contain millions of structures, yet the tools for characterizing their void spaces have not kept pace. Standard descriptors such as largest cavity diameter and pore limiting diameter are global quantities that conflate local pore geometry with inter-pore connectivity, and can hide distinct pores and network topology behind a single number. We present Mofography, an open-source Python/Rust library that recasts pore characterization as a three-dimensional image-processing problem. It segments the void space into non-overlapping pore regions, connects them at shared windows, and constructs a pore graph that decouples local properties (size, shape, chemistry) from global topology (percolation, connectivity). Global textural properties are obtained as queries on this graph and agree with those from Zeo++ and Pore-Blazer across a diverse set of metal-organic frameworks (MOFs), while remaining traceable to individual pores and windows. The same representation supports pore-resolved pore size distributions, multi-modal pore-type clustering, window detection across periodic boundaries, and percolation and accessibility analysis. To demonstrate its utility for material discovery, we develop a workflow integrated with Mofography to screen favorable pores in MOFs for xylene isomer separations and validate selected candidates with grand canonical Monte Carlo simulations. The results reveal how accessibility and competing pore environments influence whether local preferences translate into material performance. By linking global textural properties to local pore environments and their connectivity, Mofography provides a unique platform for interpreting structure–property relationships and accelerating nanoporous materials discovery.

item.title: Signed Kekulé structures and Hückel gap-closure thresholds in phenylenes
item.description: Naphthalene and biphenylene have comparable Hückel HOMO–LUMO gaps, yet no positive bond couplings close the gap of naphthalene, whereas coordinated changes of 18.9% close that of biphenylene. We define the gap-closure threshold as the smallest maximum relative change of existing bond couplings needed to close the gap. At equal reference couplings, it depends only on the signed Kekulé polynomial: it is maximal when all Kekulé structures share one sign, is fixed by a polynomial equation when one structure has the minority sign, and is otherwise bounded. Phenylenes with the same sequence of linear and angular annelations share the threshold, even when their gaps differ. For linear [N ]phenylenes it approaches π2/[4(N + 1)2]; angular [3]phenylene closes only by breaking mirror symmetry. In a bond-length model, the threshold ranks closure energies better than the relaxed gap does, and the predicted closing distortion is nearly the steepest-descent direction of the B3LYP Kohn–Sham gap (cosine 0.989).
